items.title: During Fort McCoy Prayer Breakfast, chaplain holds remembrance for 9/11 sacrifices, resilience 25 years later
items.author: Scott Sturkol
items.summary: Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, Fort McCoy community members gathered Sept. 11, 2026, to remember those who lost their lives, honor those who responded, and reflect on the resilience that continues to shape the nation.
items.body:
Twenty-five years after the terrorist attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, Fort McCoy community members gathered Sept. 11, 2026, to remember those who lost their lives, honor those who responded, and reflect on the resilience that continues to shape the nation.

During Fort McCoy’s 2026 Retiree Appreciation Day Prayer Breakfast, Chaplain (Lt. Col.) Walter McCall, Fort McCoy Garrison chaplain with the Religious Support Office, led a remembrance presentation that combined historical military records, personal reflection, and a message of hope. His presentation included a video recalling the attacks and a review of a historical report documenting the Army Reserve’s response to the events of 9/11.

McCall’s presentation connected the sacrifices of the first responders and military personnel who served that day with the continuing importance of community, healing, and resilience.

Preserving Army Reserve’s 9/11 history

McCall explained that the311th Military History Detachmentwas tasked with documenting the events in New York City, while the 90th Military History Detachment covered the Pentagon response in Washington, D.C.

The Army Reserve’s Office of Army Reserve History subsequently published two reports in 2003, including The Role of the Army Reserve in the 11 September Attacks: New York City , prepared by the 311th Military History Detachment. The reports documented the Army Reserve’s response through narrative accounts, photographs, and interviews with Reservists involved in the aftermath.

While reviewing the historical material, McCall highlighted a foreword written byLt. Gen. Thomas J. Plewes, Chief of the Army Reserve. Plewes served as chief from May 25, 1998, to May 24, 2002. The foreword in the New York report is dated May 21, 2002, rather than 2003. McCall said reading Plewes’ words helped him visualize the events of Sept. 11 and recognize the courage demonstrated by soldiers and civilians.

The foreword describes the attacks as an unimaginable national tragedy and recognizes the courage and selflessness of ordinary Americans and Army Reserve personnel. It also remembers Army Reserve soldiers who died while responding in their civilian roles, including firefighters and personnel working at the World Trade Center and Pentagon.

Remembering those who responded

McCall reviewed individual stories of Army Reserve personnel who lost their lives during the attacks.

McCall also highlighted the story of retired Col. Rick Rescorla, a Vietnam veteran and security director for Morgan Stanley at the World Trade Center. Rescorla helped evacuate thousands of employees and returned to search for people who remained in the building before losing his life. The stories illustrated the individual acts of courage and selflessness that characterized the response to the attacks.

McCall also described the Army Reserve’s broader response, which extended beyond the initial rescue efforts. Army Reserve personnel supported emergency operations, provided security, assisted civilian agencies, and mobilized to support recovery efforts.

The 311th Quartermaster Company (Mortuary Affairs), based in Aguadilla, Puerto Rico, deployed volunteers to the Pentagon within 72 hours of the attacks. Soldiers worked to recover human remains and personal effects from the debris.

The Survivor Tree: A message of hope

After discussing the lives lost and the Army Reserve’s response, McCall transitioned to a message about hope and resilience through the story of theSurvivor Treeat the World Trade Center Memorial.

The Callery pear tree had been planted in the World Trade Center plaza in 1970. During the attacks, the tree was crushed beneath steel, concrete, and burning debris. In October 2001, recovery workers discovered the damaged tree with a small cluster of green leaves.

Workers transported the tree to a nursery in the Bronx, where arborists cared for its damaged roots and helped it recover. In December 2010, the tree was returned to Lower Manhattan and replanted at the 9/11 Memorial.

McCall used the tree’s survival as a metaphor for people who have experienced trauma, loss, and hardship.

“Hope does not require complete fullness to begin,” he said. “It only requires a spark.”

He explained that even when people feel fractured, the presence of life and the ability to endure can provide the beginning of recovery.

McCall identified three spiritual lessons from the Survivor Tree:

— Sprouting from devastation:Even after profound loss and trauma, the possibility of renewal remains.

— The necessity of the nursery:Healing requires community support, care, and trusted people who help others recover.

— Carrying a scar without being defined by it:Resilience does not mean erasing the past but allowing purposeful growth to continue despite the scars.

McCall emphasized that military service members, veterans, civilians, contractors, and families can all carry visible and unseen burdens. He encouraged those attending to seek support through chaplains, behavioral health professionals, battle buddies, coworkers, family members, and veteran service organizations.

“Resilience is not an absence of scars,” McCall said. “It is a courageous decision to allow smooth, purposeful growth to flourish above all.”

Honoring sacrifice, looking to future

As his presentation concluded, McCall recognized the 2,977 people killed in the Sept. 11 attacks, including the 184 people who died at the Pentagon. He also honored the military personnel who lost their lives during the conflicts that followed and the Gold Star families who continue to carry the weight of those sacrifices.

Addressing the retirees and veterans attending the breakfast, McCall expressed gratitude for their service and contributions to the nation.

He also recognized current Soldiers, Department of the Army civilians, contractors, and families, describing each as an essential part of the military community and its continued readiness.

“To our retirees and veterans in all branches, thank you for stepping into the breach when the nation needed you most,” McCall said. “You remain a permanent, revered part of this garrison family.”

McCall concluded by asking attendees to stand for the playing ofTaps, providing a solemn close to the remembrance and an opportunity to reflect on the lives lost, the sacrifices made, and the responsibility to preserve their memory.

Twenty-five years after the attacks, his presentation connected the historical record of the Army Reserve's response with a continuing message: remembering the past, supporting one another, and finding hope through resilience.

Fort McCoy’s motto beginning in 2026 is “Training the Total Force and Shaping the Future since 1909.” The installation’s mission: “Fort McCoy strengthens Total Force Readiness by serving as a training center, Mobilization Force Generation Installation, and Strategic Support Area enabling warfighter lethality to deploy, fight, and win our nation’s wars.”

And Fort McCoy’s vision is, “To be the premier training center supporting the most capable, combat-ready, and lethal armed forces.” Located in the heart of the upper Midwest, Fort McCoy is the only U.S. Army installation in Wisconsin. The installation has provided support and facilities for the field and classroom training of more than 100,000 military personnel from all services nearly every year since 1984.

Learn more about Fort McCoy online athttps://home.army.mil/mccoy, on Facebook by searching “ftmccoy,” on Flickr at https://www.flickr.com/photos/fortmccoywi, and on X (formerly Twitter) by searching “usagmccoy.” Also try downloading the My Army Post app to your smartphone and set “Fort McCoy” or another installation as your preferred base.

Fort McCoy is also part of Army’s Installation Management Command where “We Are The Army’s Home.”

items.title: Central Oregon’s Army National Guard 1st Squadron, 82nd Cavalry Regiment, holds unit deactivation ceremony
items.author: John Hughel
items.summary: The Oregon Army National Guard's 1st Squadron, 82nd Cavalry Regiment, held its unit deactivation ceremony, while formally Casing the Colors, on September 19, 2026, in Bend, Oregon.
items.body:
As summer faded into its final golden days, the Oregon Army National Guard’s 1st Squadron, 82nd Cavalry Regiment, part of the 81st Mobile Brigade Combat Team, held a poignant Casing of Colors during the unit's deactivation ceremony and a grand Regimental Ball in Bend, Oregon, on September 19, 2026, marking the end of an era.

The Casing of Colors is a formal U.S. Army tradition in which a unit’s symbolic flags, known as colors, are lowered, furled, and placed in a protective sheath. The ritual marks the end of a unit’s active status while honoring its legacy. The 1st Squadron, 82nd Cavalry Regiment, whose streamers commemorate service in World War II, Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan, completed its final mobilization in support of the European Deterrence Initiative under Operation Atlantic Resolve, beginning in April 2021. Two waves of soldiers from the 1-82nd deployed to Poland, culminating in a final demobilization ceremony on February 4, 2023.

The official ceremony featured Col. Andrew W. Vidourek, Commander of the 82nd Brigade Troop Command, alongside Lt. Col. Richard Nicolas, Commander of the 1st Squadron, 82nd Cavalry Regiment, and Command Sgt. Maj. Jason Wilson, 1st Squadron, 82nd Cavalry. The event included a reading of the unit’s lineage and honors, the issuance of the Deactivation Order, and the casing of colors, held at the Hayden Homes Amphitheater. Later that evening, the unit held its formal “One Last Ride” Regimental Ball at the Riverhouse Convention Center.

“Today we mark the deactivation of this distinguished military unit and trace its roots back to the 1st Infantry Regiment, organized in the late 1860’s, from communities across the state in Portland, Salem, Astoria, Oregon City, Albany, and The Dalles,” said Maj. Christopher Perrotti, who served as the event narrator, while addressing the unit formation, their family members, and retired soldiers from the unit as they made this historic moment. “Beyond combat, the squadron has been a shield for the citizens of Oregon and regularly has responded to wildfires, floods, and civil unrest with speed and precision inherent to the Cavalry.”

The regiment fought in the Spanish-American War and took part in battles in the Philippines between February 1899 and July 1902. The unit saw action in World War I and received a streamer for its combat service. In World War II, the heredity included service with the 41st Infantry Division, including the lineage of A Troop and B Troop, participating in the growing campaigns of the Pacific Theatre and earning decorations for service in New Guinea, Luzon, and the Southern Philippines, and receiving the Presidential Unit Citation for exceptional meritorious service. In 2005, the unit was formally designated the 1st Squadron, 82nd Cavalry Regiment, and deployed to Iraq in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom from 2009 to 2010 and to Afghanistan in 2014-2015.

As Perroitt read the official order issued by the Secretary of the Army deactivating the unit, Soldiers stood ready to case the colors. “The Casing of the colors is a ceremony of heritage and respect. The colors represent the spirit of the unit. As they are placed in their protective cover, it signifies the unit’s mission is complete and forever engraved in the U.S. Army Cavalry history.”

On stage, the unit flag, which features yellow as the traditional color of Armor and Cavalry and symbolizes the unit’s cavalry heritage and reconnaissance role, was cased in a ceremony. The seven individual troop guidons and subsequent unit flags were also cased in sequence with meticulous care.

“Today’s ceremony marks the deactivation of 1st Squadron, 82nd Cavalry Regiment, and as mission shifts and new requirements emerge, the Army adapts,” Vidourek said. “And every so often, it reminds us that no organizational chart survives contact with the Pentagon staff officer – today’s ceremony reflects that reality.”

As Vidourek reflected on the unit’s long history and how the force structure has changed over the years, he noted it has always been defined by the men and women willing to step forward whenever Oregon and the nation needed them.

“The squadron’s colors carry honor earned by generations of troopers. Long before any of us arrived, those soldiers established standards that later generations have worked hard to uphold,” he said. “While today’s ceremony closes an important chapter, it should not be viewed as the end of the story. The Army will keep moving forward. New formations will stand up.”

Looking ahead, Vidourek stated that the new reserve center in Redmond will help the National Guard maintain a strong presence in Oregon. With the Cavalry mission departing Bend, the armory will now house soldiers from Alpha Company, 2nd Battalion, 186th Infantry.

“What gives me confidence is that while the 1st Squadron, 82nd Cavalry Regiment is deactivating, the Oregon National Guard’s presence in Central Oregon remains strong,” he said. “When the National Guard looks for a place with strong community support, exceptional training opportunities, and citizens willing to raise their right hand and serve, Central Oregon makes a compelling argument.”

In concluding his remarks, Vidourek said the unit's legacy and its place in military history will live on in each soldier.

“To the trooper standing in the formation, the squadron’s guidon may be retired, but what was built here will endure. The friendships, the lessons, the standards established, over a century of service, now belong to you to carry forward,” Vidourek said.

Lt. Col. Nicolas echoed that spirit of continued service in his remarks, noting that each soldier’s willingness to serve and their expertise are transferable skills.

“Whether you move to a new formation within the Oregon Guard, or continue to serve in another capacity, you carry the Cavalry legacy forward,” he said. “The culture that makes the 1-82 CAV special did not happen by accident. It happened because you invested in it – that investment lives on in every soldier who served under the colors. With that, thank you – Scouts Out!”

items.title: Honoring a legacy of service: Korean Service Corps exhibition opens
items.author: Hannah Cho
items.summary: A yearlong exhibition honoring the Korean Service Corps opened Sept. 18 at the UN Forces First Battle Memorial in Osan, Republic of Korea. Through artifacts, photographs and history documents, it highlights the corps' vital support to United Nations forces during the Korean War and the Korean Service Corps Battalion's continuing contribution to U.S. Army readiness and the U.S.-ROK Alliance.
items.body:
Forged in a fight for survival, the Korean Service Corps Battalion, Materiel Support Command–Korea, 19th Expeditionary Sustainment Command, has provided critical support to the U.S. Army for more than 75 years. Established during the Korean War, the organization embodies generations of Korean contributions to Army readiness and the enduring U.S.-ROK Alliance.

That shared legacy came into focus Sept. 18 as the KSC Battalion was honored during the opening of a yearlong exhibit at the UN Forces First Battle Memorial in Osan, Republic of Korea.

For the exhibit, “The Peace They Carried: The Korean Service Corps,” the battalion provided historical artifacts and materials, including an A-frame, photographs, historical documents, recruitment posters and challenge coins. Together, the items illustrate both the physical demands placed on early corps members and the evolution of the KSC from a wartime labor force into an integral part of the U.S. Army’s modern support structure in Korea.

“The title of this exhibition carries a powerful message,” said Brig. Gen. Jin H. Pak, commanding general of the 19th ESC. “During the Korean War, peace was carried not only by those who fought with weapons, but also by Korean civilians who moved ammunition and supplies, evacuated casualties, repaired defensive positions, and performed other essential duties—often under constant threat in active combat areas.”

The battalion traces its roots to the Civilian Transportation Corps, which was established during the Korean War to provide critical logistical support to United Nations forces. Using traditional Korean wooden pack frames known as jige , corps members carried ammunition, food and other supplies across rugged terrain inaccessible to vehicles.

Because the frames resembled a capital “A” against their backs, the workers became known as the “A-Frame Army.” Their difficult and often dangerous work helped keep front-line forces supplied during some of the war’s most challenging periods.

“Their courage, sacrifice and steadfast determination contributed to establishing the strong foundation of the ROK-U.S. Alliance that continues today,” Pak said.

The exhibition also recognizes the civilians whose contributions can be overshadowed in traditional accounts of the war. By preserving their stories and displaying the tools and records associated with their service, the memorial connects the sacrifices of the wartime generation with the alliance they helped build.

Osan city leadership helped establish the exhibition to honor the KSC’s wartime service, those who fought in the war’s opening battles and the members of the “A-Frame Army,” said Osan Mayor Cho Yong Ho.

“The UN Forces First Battle Memorial seeks to fill a missing page in the history of the Korean War,” Cho said.

Today, the KSC Battalion remains an essential part of the U.S. Army’s support structure on the Korean Peninsula. Its Korean national employees provide transportation, maintenance, supply, engineering and other operational support that strengthens readiness during exercises and contingencies.

The activation of the 75th KSC Truck Company April 8 at Camp Humphreys further enhanced 19th ESC’s supply and transportation capabilities. By addressing a key logistical requirement, the company provides long-haul cargo transportation that helps keep forces mobile and operational throughout the southern Korean Peninsula.

The 75th designation honors more than 75 years of Korean Service Corps members serving alongside U.S. forces. Its mission reflects how the organization has adapted to the changing needs of the Army while preserving the spirit of service on which it was founded.

The ceremony marked more than the opening of a new exhibit. It honored a shared legacy of service, partnership and sacrifice that has helped preserve peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula for generations—and continues to strengthen the alliance today.

items.title: Air Force to Get First Next-Gen Tactical C2 Centers By Year’s End
items.author: Todd South
items.summary: A single-pallet-sized tactical operations center is slated to begin shipping to 70 Air Force units by the end of the year following a recent announcement by the company that made it and the Air Force entity responsible for its development. The post Air Force to Get First Next-Gen Tactical C2 Centers By Year’s End appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —A single-pallet-sized tactical operations center is slated to begin shipping to 70 Air Force units by the end of the year following a recent announcement by the company that made it and the Air Force entity responsible for its development.

The Tactical Operations Center-Light is the Air Force’s next-generation method for conducting ground-based air battle management Several years ago, the service contracted with Lockheed Martin and L3Harris to build the first 16 prototypes of the TOC-L, which started delivering in 2023.

In 2025, though, the Air Force tapped Booz Allen Hamilton for a $315 million rapid prototyping contract to scale and produce the second iteration of the TOC-L, dubbed MR2 for Major Release 2 or Material Release 2.

The initial 16 MR1 prototypes let Airmen to get their hands on a prototype system and test it out. MR2 is the kit that will be in place to run air battle management in the near term.

“Material Release 1 is, ‘hey, how do we get the capability they need now so they can fight tonight?” Brig. Gen. Joshua Williams, program acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management, told reporters Sept. 16 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference. “Material Release 2 is focused on deeper integration, improved edge connectivity, and more mature support.”

The system connects to all major aircraft and capabilities the Air Force deploys and can work backward-compatible through the DAF Battle Network, Patrick Hamilton, vice president for defense technology at Booz, told Air & Space Forces Magazine at the conference.

“This is the next-generation C2 system that the Air Force is going to deploy that hopefully will be in place for the next 30 to 40 years for the new C2 fight,” Hamilton said.

Because the TOC-L system can incorporate software changes more readily than legacy ground systems such as the Control and Reporting Center, it can more quickly add in capabilities, applications, and other items from the DAF Battle Network as it grows and more options are added.

“That is the fundamental difference to the prior prototype,” Hamilton said. “Now you’ll be able to, in the future, iterate as future improvements go online in the Battle Network.”

Operational Air Force units have spent the past year taking and testing TOC-L systems “downrange,” Col. Bai Lan Zhu, senior materiel leader for the Advanced Battle Management System, told reporters during the conference media session.

The total number of TOC-Ls to flow across the entire Air Force is still evolving, Zhu said.

“The exact quantities are something that the operational community is going to refine over time,” she said.

The first wave of TOC-Ls will begin shipping to units by or before December. The company plans to deliver 70 units under the current contract, Hamilton said.

The new system can also draw from at least three “enclaves” of data, letting users fuse information from both classified and unclassified sources more easily.

“So, if you have something coming in, let’s say from an FAA unclassified radar, and you want to put that on the situational awareness [common operating picture] that the user is looking at, which is in a secret enclave, you need the ability to move that data up,” Hamilton said.

The TOC-L provides that ability.

The system can also render those enclaves unclassified when powered off, based on National Security Agency data-at-rest standards.

In the past, system users would spend hours at the end of each mission or shift physically removing a series of drives, labeling them and storing them according to protocols, only to have to rebuild the setup the next day, Mike Lewis, Booz’s chief engineer for TOC-L, told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

“There are a lot of logistics and risk in that type of scenario, so with data at rest being unclassified, it’s a real key to making this tactically relevant from a speed perspective and from a cyber perspective,” Lewis said.

Fewer Pieces, Fewer People

TOC-L replaces the Cold War-era Control and Reporting Center, previously centered around the trusty but bulky AN/TPS-75 radar system.

The legacy system required as many as six C-17 Globemaster IIIs to transport all of its components, using radar dishes, heavy vehicles, and nearly two dozen power generators.

The CRC would require hundreds of Airmen to set up and operate and could take between 24 and 72 hours to set up and tear down.

TOC-L is a feather by comparison.

It fits on a single pallet, with one additional pallet to hold its generator; can be transported inside a single C-130 Hercules; requires about 10 Airmen to operate; and can be set up or torn down in less than an hour.

The TOC-L can squeeze into such a small frame and use far fewer people, partly because of advances in electronics and partly because it can tap into the DAF Battle Network and other networks to access radar and other feeds instead of carrying its own radars into the fight.

The shift in allowing nonproprietary equipment to hook into the TOC-L system also drastically trims down the amount of hardware needed to operate the system’s crucial functions, Hamilton told Air & Space Forces Magazine.

“We’re going to collect iterative feedback from ABMS and the user community as it deploys all over the world,” said Hamilton. “And I think over the next 12 to 24 months, that will start to define what [Material Release 3] will look like and what we hear from the user community, what they prioritize for.”

items.title: Advancing digital health: Navy Medicine’s Health 1nformaticist of the Month helps shape operational medicine
items.author: Arsenio R. Cortez Jr.
items.summary: From shipboard data platforms to tactical field networks, Lt. Cmdr. Harley T. Sheffield is transforming how the Navy and Marine Corps deliver digital health care at the tip of the spear. For his efforts, Sheffield was named Navy Medicine's Health Informaticist of the Month for September.
items.body:
From shipboard data platforms to tactical field networks, Lt. Cmdr. Harley T. Sheffield is transforming how the Navy and Marine Corps deliver digital health care at the tip of the spear. For his efforts, Sheffield was named Navy Medicine's Health Informaticist of the Month for September.

As the chief nursing informatics officer for Naval Medical Forces Pacific, Sheffield spent the last year translating frontline clinical realities into critical technical requirements. His mission is advancing and evaluating digital health capabilities across Navy and Marine Corps operational environments.

As a Navy nurse informaticist, Sheffield knows firsthand what it is like to provide patient care on the front lines, a clinical background that directly influences how he evaluates new technology in the field.

“I don’t just ask whether the software works,” Sheffield said. “I look at it through the lens of the functional user. I ask whether it will work for an operational user with minimal resources, limited communications, and in environments ranging from the middle of the ocean to the desert. Ultimately, I ask whether this is a tool I can realistically use to deliver and document care in a way that benefits the operational commander, the unit, the provider, and most importantly, the patient.”

Throughout 2026, he led and supported health informatics efforts aboard USSEssex(LHD-2) and during the Marine Corps Integrated Training Exercise (ITX) at Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center (MCAGCC), Twentynine Palms, California, ensuring emerging technologies were assessed not only for technical performance, but also for their ability to safely, effectively, and reliably support the warfighter.

"Lt. Sheffield combines a high degree of informatics knowledge with a willingness to work hard and take ownership of problems," said Capt. Christopher Phillips, chief medical officer for NMFP. "He is a respected resource within the informatics community because of his dedication and ability to work with others on the team as they work to make our operational electronic health record as safe, effective, and user-friendly as possible."

Sheffield’s impact to the fleet was demonstrated during the USSEssexOperational Medicine Clinical Data Platform (OPMED CDP) evaluation. Serving as the action officer, Sheffield was responsible for coordinating multiple supporting units and personnel to complete system installation and operational implementation in a shipboard environment. He coordinated cross-functional teams for system installation and validation, user training, clinical workflow evaluation, data quality review, and assessment of more than 100 historical and newly identified system issues. His hands-on leadership led to the successful testing of data seeding while underway, demonstrating the platform’s ability to support operationally relevant deployment conditions and informing evaluation of system reliability, usability, and readiness. His findings directly informed the operational go/no-go decision and produced actionable recommendations to improve patient safety, data fidelity, and overall system readiness prior to broader fleet deployment.

Sheffield also supported the Theater Blood (TBLD) operational experiment conducted duringthe RIMPAC 2026aboard the USSEsse x and across multiple units while underway, coordinating efforts among operational units, clinical subject matter experts, blood program personnel, and technical teams to evaluate digital blood management capabilities in a realistic maritime operational environment. This distributed assessment identified more than 50 findings related to blood product accountability, donor management, traceability, auditability, data accuracy, and command visibility. His contributions provided critical operational insights that will shape future distributed maritime operations and expeditionary medical readiness.

From the sea to the Twentynine Palms, California desert, Sheffield’s work continued to impact warfighter readiness. Sheffield served as an evaluation lead during the Marine Corps Integrated Training Exercise (ITX) Operational Medicine Pilot at MCAGCC, where the Battlefield Assisted Trauma Distributed Observation Kit-Joint (BATDOK-J), Operational Medicine Care Delivery Platform (OPMED CDP), OPMED CDP Web, Medical Hub, and MHS GENESIS were assessed across realistic Marine Corps medical workflows.

The pilot tracked digital documentation under operationally relevant conditions from the point of injury through Role 1 and Role 2 care and into enterprise systems. A key achievement of the exercise was production testing with live patient records on the Marine Corps Enterprise Tactical Network in a field setting. Sheffield helped test and train more than 50 personnel, supported execution of multiple operational mission threads, and enabled controlled production encounters that demonstrated both the promise of an integrated digital health ecosystem and the operational gaps requiring continued improvement.

When considering what these technological innovations actually mean for an 18-year-old corpsman in a field operation or the patient being treated, Sheffield emphasizes practical support over complexity.

"The technology is not here to change operational medicine," Sheffield said. "Instead, it is a tool to enhance the care and decision-making of the corpsman already doing the job. Quick-reference information, timestamps, and visibility across the continuum can help a corpsman identify potential gaps in care, reassess what has already been done, and recognize when additional support may be needed."

When the tactical situation allows, electronic documentation can follow the patient from the earliest stages of care through definitive treatment, while also giving commanders command-and-control visibility to identify urgent needs like medical assistance, evacuation, or resupply.

"Ultimately, all of this benefits the patient by reducing potential gaps in care, improving continuity, and ensuring that care delivered in the operational environment becomes part of the patient’s longitudinal health record," he said.

Across these diverse environments, Sheffield has bridged the gap between technology and the warfighter by translating frontline clinical experience into clear technical and operational requirements. His work reflects the essential role of health informatics in ensuring digital health capabilities are not merely fielded, but are safe, usable, interoperable, and operationally relevant to the Sailors and Marines who depend on them. His work had advanced operational medicine modernization, earning him the Health Informaticist of the Month for the Bureau of Medicine and Surgery (BUMED) health informatics directorate.

NMFP provides oversight for 10 Navy Medicine Readiness and Training Commands (NMRTC) on the West Coast and Pacific Rim that train, man and equip medical forces, primarily in military treatment facilities. Globally, NMFP oversees eight research laboratories that deliver research expertise in support of warfighter health and readiness. Additionally, NMFP manages the Naval Expeditionary Medicine Warfighter Development Center (NEMWDC), which plays a critical role in preparing medical teams for expeditionary and operational environments.

Navy Medicine, with more than 44,000 military and civilian health care professionals, provides expeditionary medical support to the warfighter.

items.title: America's Contingency Corps trains against the drone threat of the next war
items.author: Courtesy
items.summary: Scarlet Dragon 26-3, conducted Sept. 11-17, 2026, at Fort Bragg, brought XVIII Airborne Corps Soldiers and industry partners together to evaluate emerging technologies against realistic unmanned aircraft threats. The exercise integrated sensors, electronic warfare, artificial intelligence, resilient data pathways, autonomous systems, command-and-control capabilities and defensive fires to determine how layered systems can detect, track and defeat increasingly complex drone threats, including lar
items.body:
FORT BRAGG, N.C. — The character of warfare is changing, and the growing use of unmanned aircraft systems on battlefields around the world is forcing militaries to adapt faster than ever.

At Fort Bragg, the XVIII Airborne Corps is taking on that challenge through Scarlet Dragon, an exercise that brings Soldiers and industry partners together to test emerging technology in realistic field conditions. The exercise helped the corps evaluate which capabilities can integrate across the force, including systems designed to detect, track and defeat unmanned aircraft threats.

“The Scarlet Dragon exercise has become a validation exercise in the dirt with Soldiers doing integrated, real-world operational-type tasks,” said Col. Tom Monahan, director of the XVIII Airborne Corps’ Joint Innovation Outpost.

The exercise, held Sept. 11-17, 2026, at Fort Bragg, combined Soldiers, military systems, artificial intelligence, resilient data pathways and industry partners to address one of the Army’s most pressing challenges: integrating sensors, electronic warfare, command-and-control and defensive fires against evolving unmanned aircraft threats.

“Basically, transitioning gaps to capability requirements that we need, capabilities that will fill the gaps, and then running them through the exercise and the experimentation to come away with our findings to support the warfighter,” said Col. Paul Staeheli, the XVIII Airborne Corps operations officer.

Rather than testing technology in isolation, Scarlet Dragon places emerging capabilities in an austere field environment where Soldiers can evaluate how they perform against realistic threats and operational problems.

The exercise replicates tactics and capabilities Soldiers could encounter on a future battlefield, including large-scale drone swarms and systems modeled after threats seen in current conflicts. Some scenarios feature swarms of up to 100 unmanned aircraft, giving Soldiers the opportunity to train against the scale and complexity of modern drone attacks.

That threat environment allows the Corps to evaluate not only individual systems, but also how different capabilities work together.

“What we’ve found is that there’s no one sensor to rule them all,” said Col. Rob Kenny, the XVIII Airborne Corps chief of fires. “It takes an integrated, layered approach. Here at the company node, we’re working on: can we sense, can we make sense, and can we pass that information back to give time and space for our Soldiers to act?”

Electronic warfare, sensors, radar, autonomous systems and defensive fires each provide different tools for detecting, identifying and defeating unmanned aircraft. Integrating those capabilities is critical as adversaries continue to evolve their use of drones.

Scarlet Dragon also demonstrates how the Army can work with industry to develop and integrate new technology faster.

Leading-edge technology companies are working alongside Soldiers to identify operational problems, test potential solutions and gather feedback directly from the field. The partnership gives developers firsthand insight into how their systems perform in realistic military environments while giving Soldiers an opportunity to shape the technologies they may eventually use.

“The vendors out here are different contractors with different companies trying to show the limitations and capabilities of all their systems,” said Staff Sgt. Charles Johnson, noncommissioned officer in charge of the G34 company node. “They’re giving the full scope of what their systems can do and how it can help us in the best way possible.”

The effort extends beyond developing new equipment. The exercise examines the broader counter-UAS challenge, from passive detection technologies such as acoustic sensors and portable radar to autonomous systems and emerging capabilities designed specifically for the UAS fight.

That approach reflects the Corps’ broader responsibility as America’s Contingency Corps.

The exercise also reinforces a larger message about modernization: preparing for the future battlefield requires more than buying new equipment. It requires understanding emerging threats, testing solutions under realistic conditions and rapidly adapting when those solutions fall short.

Through experimentation and collaboration with industry, the XVIII Airborne Corps is working to integrate autonomous technologies with legacy systems and address a rapidly evolving unmanned aircraft threat.

The goal is not simply to observe the future of warfare, but to prepare for it.

As unmanned systems continue to reshape battlefields around the world, exercises such as Scarlet Dragon give the corps an opportunity to learn, adapt and develop the capabilities Soldiers will need to maintain an advantage in future conflicts.

The XVIII Airborne Corps will continue to validate these systems in April 2027 during Scarlet Dragon 27-1, preparing for the larger Summit Strike exercise at Fort Drum, New York, in September 2027.

items.title: Massachusetts Guard Gets First F-35 to Replace Departed F-15s
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: The Massachusetts Air National Guard’s 104th Fighter Wing received its first F-35A Joint Strike Fighter on Sept. 13, becoming the latest unit to get its hands on the new fifth-generation jet. The post Massachusetts Guard Gets First F-35 to Replace Departed F-15s appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Massachusetts Air National Guard’s 104th Fighter Wing received its first F-35A Joint Strike Fighter on Sept. 13, becoming the latest unit to get its hands on the new fifth-generation jet.

The 104th, located at Barnes Air National Guard Base, is replacing its legacy F-15 Eagle fighters with the F-35 and held a ceremony to officially welcome the fifth-generation jet with officials including Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey and National Guard Bureau Chief Air Force Gen. Steven Nordhaus, the Guard said in a Sept. 14 release.

“For generations, men and women at the 104th Fighter Wing have answered the call, protected the skies, served our state and defended our country,” Healey said. “The arrival of the F-35A represents a new chapter for this great military installation here. And it’s also an affirmation of the extraordinary professionalism and readiness of this wing that has existed decade after decade after decade.”

Military officials, Massachusetts leaders, lawmakers, and local civic partners have worked for a decade to bring the F-35 to Barnes. The Guard officially decided to bring the F-35A to Barnes in December 2024, and the base has been preparing for its arrival for the last several years. Barnes’ preparation for the F-35 included building infrastructure such as sunshades, acquiring the necessary equipment, and training Airmen to be ready to fly and sustain the jets.

The 104th’s last three F-15s departed Barnes in October 2025. One of those pilots, Capt. Kyle “Nuke” Eckert, is now an F-35 pilot with the wing.

“It was an honor to be part of the final three-ship of Eagles to leave Barnes back in October of 2025,” Eckert said. “To now be one of the first F-35A pilots at Barnes Air National Guard Base is an amazing full circle moment.”

Col. Michael “Shot” Glass, who took command of the 104th in December, said the new fifth-generation jets “provides our wing with increase and unmatched capabilities to safeguard both our country and the great city of Westfield as we execute our new 104th Fighter Wing mission and vision.”

The 104th’s former commander, Brig. Gen. David “Moon” Halasi-Kun, also emphasized what the F-35 is able to do.

“The F-35A brings with it incredible capabilities that will be able to support combatant commanders around the world, as well as continued defense of the United States from our 24-hour alert site,” Halasi-Kun said. “I know that our [Airmen] will be up to the challenge as we start to begin our conversion.”

Barnes is now the 15th base across the Air Force to host the F-35, and fifth Guard base. Misawa Air Base in Japan also got its first F-35 in 2026, and Kingsley Field, Ore., is slated to receive its first jets in summer 2027.

items.title: Meet NMRTC Twentynine Palms Junior Civilian of the 3rd Quarter: Meredith Jones
items.author: Christopher Jones
items.summary: Navy Medicine Readiness and Training Command Twentynine Palms recognized Meredith Jones, an occupational health technician at Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms, as its Junior Civilian of the Quarter for the third quarter of 2026. Jones supports the health and readiness of active-duty service members and civilian employees through medical surveillance screenings and occupational health programs, including hearing conservation.
items.body:
TWENTYNINE PALMS, Calif. — Navy Medicine Readiness and Training Command Twentynine Palms recently recognized Meredith Jones, an occupational health technician at Naval Hospital Twentynine Palms, as its Junior Civilian of the Quarter for the third quarter of 2026.

Jones, a native of Guilford, Connecticut, works within the directorate of public health, conducting medical surveillance health screenings and examinations for active-duty service members and civilian employees across Marine Corps Air Ground Combat Center Twentynine Palms.

“We screen employees and service members to ensure individuals are fit to perform their jobs and monitor personnel exposed to hazardous environments to ensure long-term workplace safety,” said Jones.

Her work includes audiograms, vision screenings, spirometry and electrocardiograms, helping the occupational health department identify potential health concerns and support the readiness of the installation’s workforce.

“These exams directly support the mission by ensuring our warfighters and employees are medically ready to deploy and complete their duties across the installation,” Jones said.

Of her responsibilities, Jones said supporting the hearing conservation program is among the most rewarding. The program monitors personnel exposed to hazardous noise and provides education aimed at preventing occupational hearing loss.

“I find being part of the hearing conservation program rewarding because I help protect service members and civilian employees from preventable, permanent hearing loss caused by hazardous noise in the workplace,” Jones said. “Annual screenings and hearing protection education are important tools to actively preserve hearing, medical readiness and quality of life for our patients.”

For Jones, the importance of protecting hearing is also personal, having seen the impact of hearing loss within her own family.

“My mom experienced hearing loss from the use of chemotherapy and now relies on hearing aids. Her experience has shown me how important it is not to take our hearing for granted,” said Jones. “While her hearing loss was unavoidable, many work-related cases can be prevented with the proper precautions. I find it fulfilling to provide this support and care within my role in occupational health.”

Her studies in human services at Loyola University Chicago, along with previous experience in behavioral health, pediatrics and education, helped prepare Jones to work in public health and strengthened her approach to supporting patients from a variety of backgrounds.

Jones also has a personal connection to the Navy and Marine Corps through her family. Her maternal grandfather served in the Navy and fought in the Pacific during World War II, while her paternal grandfather served in the Marine Corps.

“Being able to support both branches here on this installation is very fulfilling to me,” Jones said.

For Jones, being named Junior Civilian of the Quarter is recognition of work centered on supporting the people who carry out the mission each day.

“It is an honor to support our workforce, those who make the mission possible, and it is also an honor to have my efforts recognized by my leadership,” Jones said.

Outside of work, Jones enjoys traveling, attending concerts, reading and spending time with her dog, family and friends.

For others working in healthcare and support roles, Jones emphasized the importance of recognizing the impact their everyday work can have.

“The work we do matters,” Jones said. “Take pride in doing your job well, supporting others, and knowing that your dedication makes a meaningful difference to those we serve and the mission we support.”

items.author: Keith Goodsell
items.summary: NAVAL STATION NORFOLK, Va. – The Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Stout (DDG 55) departed Naval Station Norfolk, Sept. 21, 2026, to begin deployment operations.
items.body:
NAVAL STATION NORFOLK, Va. – The Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Stout (DDG 55) departed Naval Station Norfolk, Sept. 21, 2026, to begin deployment operations.

The warship’s departure comes after months of training, maintenance, and certification events.

“The crew of USS Stout trained relentlessly to ensure our warship is prepared to execute prompt and sustained operations," said Cmdr. Kevin Taylor, commanding officer, USS Stout (DDG 55). “We built a culture of sustained readiness and resilience and are fully prepared to sail forward, defend our nation's interests, and execute our mission at the absolute highest standard of excellence."

USS Stout is a multi-mission surface combatant capable of conducting anti-air, anti-submarine, and anti-surface warfare operations. Commissioned in 1994, Stout is the fifth warship of the Arleigh Burke class and belongs to the class's baseline Flight I configuration. The warship is named after World War II Navy Cross recipient Rear Admiral Herald F. Stout, who heroically commanded the Fletcher class destroyer USS Claxton (DD 571) during the Battle of Bougainville.

Commander, Naval Surface Force Atlantic is responsible for manning, training, and equipping assigned surface forces and shore activities, ensuring a capable and combat-ready force to support U.S. national interests. The SURFLANT force consists of more than 66 warships and 34 shore commands.

For more information about SURFLANT, visit Facebook.com/SURFLANT or http://www.surflant.usff.navy.mil/.

items.title: General Atomics delivers FQ-42 Vengeance to Nevada air base
items.author: Cristina Stassis
items.summary: Creech Air Force Base received a new FQ-42 Vengeance aircraft on Friday, with the jet to continue regular test and evaluation operations.
items.body:
MilTech

General Atomics delivers FQ-42 Vengeance to Nevada air base

General Atomics FQ-42 Vengeance flies alongside an F-35 and an F-15E. (General Atomics)

A Nevada Air Force Base was picked to house General Atomics’ FQ-42, a week after the U.S. Air Force dubbed the Collaborative Combat Aircraft as Vengeance .

On Friday, a new FQ-42 Vengeance aircraft was delivered to Creech Air Force Base, according to a Monday company release , and will continue regular test and evaluation operations to experiment with the new jet.

“Every week, the Air Force is pushing forward with new and more impressive accomplishments using Vengeance. It’s amazing to think of how far this program has come in such a short amount of time,” Vice President of Advanced Programs Mike Atwood said in the release.

The announcement follows two months after Creech conducted an Agile Combat Employment exercise using Anduril’s FQ-44 Fury , allowing airmen to carry out sorties and build foundational tactics and procedures that will mold how CCA are integrated into the force.

Anduril has yet to announce which Air Force base will house Fury.

Vengeance, which has an internal weapons bay and other low observability and boosted survivability features, flew alongside F-35 and F-15E Strike Eagles in preparation for collaborative control operations with manned aircraft, per the statement.

Recently, Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink revealed that the service expects to have at least 500 autonomous aircraft in service by 2032, with them meant to perform many of the same missions manned fighters complete currently.

“By then, our special operators will have the ability to employ thousands of autonomous one-way attack systems, and we will have autonomous fighters like the Collaborative Combat Aircraft,” Meink said during last week’s keynote address at the Air & Space Forces Association’s 2026 Air, Space & Cyber Conference.

General Atomics said the company completed a new “low-observable paint facility” aimed at supporting CCA production with increased manufacturing space, and the company is on track to deliver six aircraft per month.

Vengeance’s production is underway on General Atomics’ dime as “government funding plans mature,” per the statement, in an effort to prevent delays in delivery.

The service’s fiscal 2027 request included $996.5 million in procurement funding for the CCA program. It also requests $150 million in advanced procurement for the following fiscal year and $1.37 billion in continued research and development. The total program request is $2.37 billion.

items.title: From Lab to Launch — NPS Accelerates Technology Transition
items.author: Matthew Schehl
items.summary: Innovation at the Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) does not end when a research project is completed or a patent is awarded. Transforming an idea from a creative spark in the lab into a game-changing capability in the hands of a warfighter requires a seamless transition between academia, military and industry.
items.body:
Innovation at the Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) does not end when a research project is completed or a patent is awarded. Transforming an idea from a creative spark in the lab into a game-changing capability in the hands of a warfighter requires a seamless transition between academia, military and industry.

NPS excels at this.

Through its Emerging Technology and Innovation Office (ETIO), part of the Office of Research and Innovation (ORI), NPS serves as a bridge between government research and private sector innovation, helping identify pathways for technologies developed by faculty and students to mature into products and services with military and commercial value.

By working closely with the institution’s Partnership Intermediary Agreement (PIA) organizations — including Fleetwerx, the Naval Postgraduate School Foundation and TechLink — NPS connects researchers with entrepreneurs, investors and companies interested in developing new capabilities.

This technology transfer is a critical component of the Department of the Navy innovation ecosystem. It enables federal laboratories and research institutions to collaborate with industry through agreements that allow for the exchange of expertise, testing opportunities and intellectual property.

"We engage with non-federal entities to promote technologies that have been developed at our labs,” said Agata Maslowska, NPS technology transfer lead. “The goal is to improve technologies that we developed, or evaluate commercial technologies that already exist, and determine how they can be scaled to meet military needs.”

ETIO facilitates several mechanisms that help bridge the gap between research and operational application. While Cooperative Research and Development Agreements, or CRADAs, provide a framework for the execution of research between NPS and non-federal entities, the institution has developed critical mechanisms with its PIA partners to ensure key innovations don’t just stay in the lab.

“Part of the question is, how do we actually get technology into the hands of the warfighter?” said Kaitie Penry, Director of Emerging Technology and Innovation within ORI. “There are several different pathways, and technology transfer helps enable that transition.”

One pathway involves licensing NPS-developed intellectual property to companies that can further develop, manufacture and ultimately deliver products back to government customers. In addition, with the help of its PIA partners, ETIO facilitates more direct engagement with potential partners who can help mature research into market-ready solutions.

To support that effort, NPS launched a series of “From Lab to Launch” Reverse Pitch events, the next of which is BlueTech Nexus, slated for Sept. 22 at Hopkins Marine Station in Monterey.

This reverse pitch event will convene strategic investors, maritime technology companies, defense integrators and Navy stakeholders to preview a select portfolio of NPS patented technologies available for licensing, with a focus on autonomy, AI, sensing and maritime systems.

BlueTech Nexus will also feature a new collaboration with California State University Monterey Bay (CSUMB). Students in a business-oriented commercialization course are helping transform technical research into market-focused presentations designed to resonate with investors and technology companies.

Unlike traditional pitch events where startups seek investment, NPS researchers present technologies directly to industry representatives, venture capital firms and prospective commercialization partners at these “From Lab to Launch” events.

And these efforts have proven successful. NPS’ first reverse pitch event back in 2025 resulted in one of the largest licensing returns in school history, demonstrating the value of connecting innovators directly with the commercial marketplace.

“The highlight was a piece of technology where the co-inventor was a student,” Penry said. “It really shows why NPS can make a difference when you have the warfighter in the room doing the research and developing the technology.”

That combination of student operational experience and faculty defense expertise remains one of NPS’ greatest strengths. Military students arrive on campus directly from operational assignments and bring firsthand knowledge of challenges confronting the fleet and joint force. Working alongside faculty researchers, they help develop practical solutions shaped by real-world requirements.

“Our students come from the fleet,” Maslowska said. “They know what is needed to improve operations, and their input is incredibly valuable.”

Many NPS inventions include student co-inventors, underscoring the institution's unique role in combining education, research and operational relevance.

“It reinforces the credibility of the research and education conducted here at NPS,” Penry said. “The more our technologies are wanted out in the community, the more it shows that what we are doing here has an impact on national security.”

One of the most significant recent opportunities for expanding technology transition has been the U.S. Department of War’s Defense Patent Holiday initiative. The program allows companies to obtain Commercial Evaluation Licenses (CELs) for no fee, giving them an opportunity to evaluate patented government technologies before committing to full licensing agreements.

The initiative lowers barriers for industry to explore federal innovations while creating new pathways for technology transition, commercialization and eventual fielding.

To date, 25 Defense Patent Holiday CELs have been executed across the military services, and 14 of them are from Navy organizations. Of those, impressively, 10 originate from NPS technologies. Those licenses represent companies across the defense, aerospace, space systems, communications, advanced technology and energy sectors.

While some defense laboratories have participated selectively, NPS embraced the initiative as an opportunity to increase visibility for its research portfolio and accelerate transition opportunities.

“It’s a lot of work, but it’s worth the investment,” Maslowska said. “We’ve already seen tremendous interest in our technologies.” That interest is reflected in the technologies attracting the greatest commercial attention.

The clear leader is NPS’ Mixed Reality technology portfolio, which has generated four executed CELs and another currently in process. Originally developed to support training and quality assurance applications, the technology is drawing interest for defense readiness, aviation flight training, workflow guidance, logistics operations, manufacturing training and human-machine teaming applications.

“What is fascinating is how many different applications companies see in the same technology,” Maslowska said. “There are so many different ways they want to utilize it.”

The second most sought-after technology is NPS’ Phase Change Composite thermal management technology, which currently has two executed CELs and two more pending. Potential applications include spacecraft thermal management, thermal energy storage, expeditionary power systems, off-grid energy generation, disaster response support and infrastructure temperature regulation.

Another emerging technology attracting significant attention is the Extended Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) Network, an artificial intelligence and machine learning capability developed at NPS. The technology has already generated one executed CEL and two additional licenses in process. Companies are exploring applications ranging from hyperspectral imagery analysis and automatic target recognition to anomaly detection, healthcare analytics, energy exploration and mining operations.

Taken together, current licensing activity indicates concentrated demand in four major areas: immersive training and mixed reality, thermal management and energy storage, artificial intelligence for sensing and analytics, and space and remote-sensing technologies.

The growing interest demonstrates the broader relevance of research conducted at NPS, where technologies designed to solve military challenges often possess significant commercial potential as well.

“NPS and other DON laboratories are vital for fostering innovation that can develop capabilities for military needs,” said Dr. Maddie Mettler, technology manager with TechLink. “To move those innovations to market, we need to bring industry partners to the table.”

“The tech transfer ecosystem empowers industry partners to harness the research investment DON labs like NPS have made to increase the speed at which technology can be delivered to the warfighter and adapted for civilian use,” she continued. “Events like BlueTech Nexus and new initiatives such as the Defense Patent Holiday are bringing technology transfer to the forefront in the DON.”

As NPS’ ETIO continues to create opportunities for the rapid transition of NPS-developed technologies, such as the upcoming BlueTech Nexus, the institution is expanding the network needed to transition promising technologies beyond the research stage. “The opportunity right now is to make those technologies matter,” Maslowska said. “To make them into something that both the U.S. economy and the warfighter can benefit from.”

By connecting military operators, faculty researchers, industry partners and investors, NPS is helping accelerate the innovation process and shorten the distance between discovery and deployment.

In doing so, the university is demonstrating that the true measure of innovation is not simply a patent on the wall, but a capability delivered to those who need it most.

NPS, located in Monterey, California, provides warfighting-focused graduate education, including classified studies and interdisciplinary research, to advance the operational effectiveness, technological leadership and warfighting advantage of the naval service. Established in 1909, NPS offers master’s, doctoral and distance-learning certificate programs to U.S. Department of War military and civilian students, as well as to international partners, to develop warfighters and leaders who can think critically, solve complex operational problems and deliver mission-ready solutions through advanced education and research.

items.title: SDA Seeks to Expand Ground Architecture for Future Missile Tracking Satellites
items.author: Courtney Albon
items.summary: The Space Development Agency is opening a competition to expand its ground architecture to support a growing fleet of missile warning, tracking, and defense satellites. The post SDA Seeks to Expand Ground Architecture for Future Missile Tracking Satellites appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

The Space Development Agency is opening a competition to expand its ground architecture to support a growing fleet of missile warning, tracking, and defense satellites.

The agency issued a solicitation Sept. 18 requesting bids from companies to develop ground entry points for its missile defense satellites at locations around the world. By early next year, SDA plans to choose a single company to build, install, and maintain up to eight new ground entry points and to perform upgrades at current sites.

The ground segment expansion will support Tranche 3 of what SDA calls its Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture , a low-Earth orbit constellation envisioned to include hundreds of data transport and missile tracking satellites that will be refreshed every two years with new capability. So far, SDA has launched just eight missile tracking satellites as part of what it calls “Tranche 0” to demonstrate the viability of space-based missile tracking in LEO. The agency is in the midst of launching Tranche 1, which will feature 28 missile warning and tracking satellites. Tranche 2 will include 54, and Tranche 3 will have 108 spacecraft.

That proliferated space architecture requires a network of ground systems that can push data from satellites to military users who need it to inform decisions about how to respond to missile threats. SDA expects that distributing those ground systems across multiple locations will both improve the performance of the capability and make it more resilient.

For its first two operational tranches, SDA is requiring its satellite vendors to provide the ground stations needed to operate their spacecraft. General Dynamics Mission Systems is under contract to integrate those ground stations into ground operations centers, which serve as hubs for each tranche of satellites. SDA has awarded the company $816 million to date for that work.

For Tranche 3, the agency wants to transition to an enterprise model, according to a Government Accountability Office report issued in January. That approach would feature “new capabilities” and build on the earlier tranches. SDA has also selected SAIC to serve as a third-party integrator for Tranche 3, which GAO says should help address past challenges with ground system testing and operations.

SDA expects to start launching Tranche 3 satellites in late 2028 or 2029, but in the meantime it’s focused on populating Tranche 1. The agency has launched three batches of data transport satellites and has six missions left to complete the tranche. SDA Director Gurpartap Sandhoo told reporters Sept. 15 at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference that the first Tranche 1 tracking satellites should launch either late this year or early next .

The Space Force’s fiscal 2027 budget requests $3.5 billion for SDA’s LEO-based Resilient Missile Warning/Missile Tracking program. Budget documents indicate that fiscal ‘27 funding, if approved, will support early work on Tranche 3 ground entry points and other infrastructure to expand the “global footprint.”

When Space Force leaders started talking about expanding the service early this year, the idea was simple: double the size of the force in the next five years. At AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference this week, officials detailed just how they’re planning to grow so much so quickly.

The Space Force revealed this week that it has space control weapons on orbit, but the head of U.S. Space Command said the U.S. still has “a long way to go” in improving its ability to detect and target threats in the domain.

As the Space Force prepares to field new fleets of satellites that can track moving targets in the air and on the ground, it’s working to ensure it has the organizational structures in place to onboard and operate those systems.

The Space Force estimates about 10 percent of its programs will be impacted under a continuing resolution for the coming fiscal year, according to Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess.

Guardians are playing a critical role in U.S. operations against Iran, providing electronic warfare effects to stifle enemy air defense and communication systems and other space capabilities vital to the war effort, Gen. Douglas Schiess said in one of his first appearances since swearing in as Chief of Space Operations.

items.title: Marine Leaders Forge Joint Bonds in Kings Bay, Earn Honorary CPO Anchor
items.author: Ashley Berumen
items.summary: Two senior enlisted Marines complete traditional six-week Chief Petty Officer Initiation with nearly 90 Navy chief selects in Kings Bay, Georgia.
items.body:
KINGS BAY, Ga. — Guided by the shared core values of honor, courage and commitment and an effort to strengthen joint-service cohesiveness, two Marine Corps Security Force Battalion (MCSFBn) Kings Bay leaders recently completed the Navy’s demanding Chief Petty Officer Initiation, earning the title of honorary chief.

On Sept. 16, Sgt. Maj. Cory Daly and 1st Sgt. Brandon Andrade joined nearly 90 chief selects across Naval Submarine Base Kings Bay as they received their chief anchors and combination covers. Completion of the initiation, known as CPOI, marked their honorary induction into the Chiefs Mess, an accomplishment only a select group of Marines have achieved in the battalion’s history.

Each year, when first class petty officers receive notification of their selection to chief petty officer, naval commands across the fleet kick off a rigorous initiation for “chief selects.” The Navy’s CPOI, often referred to as "chief season," is deeply rooted in naval tradition. For six weeks, Navy senior enlisted leaders instill a sense of pride in naval heritage, foster deep trust among peers, and provide invaluable mentorship needed to forge the next generation of deckplate leaders, culminating in the chief pinning ceremony.

Daly said he was grateful for the opportunity to experience CPOI alongside Kings Bay chief selects.

“The Chiefs Mess is deeply ingrained in Navy culture. There is a strong sense of identity, camaraderie, and shared responsibility that comes with being part of it,” said Daly. “We don’t have anything quite like that formally established within the Marine Corps or at the battalion level.”

Master Chief Master-at-Arms Jeffrey J. Harris, MCSFBn Kings Bay’s senior enlisted advisor, emphasized the rarity of cross-service participation.

“Marines have their own separate promotion and staff noncommissioned officer development traditions,” said Harris. “It is very rare for a U.S. Marine to go through the U.S. Navy's Chief Petty Officer Initiation process.”

Andrade received the title of honorary chief last December when he graduated from the Navy Senior Enlisted Academy, but he insisted on experiencing the physical and mental demands of CPOI firsthand.

“When I returned from the academy, I asked the Chiefs Mess to put me through chief season,” said Andrade. “I did it for the experience and hoped to gain a new leadership perspective.”

With 41 years of military service between the two of them, neither Daly nor Andrade is new to leadership roles, but Daly said the last six weeks have given him an opportunity to reflect on his own leadership style.

“I realize a lot of the tasks and ideas behind chief season are not meant for an E-8, let alone an E-9, just given our experience level,” said Daly. “This has been a humbling experience that has required a lot of self-reflection. It’s challenged me to identify areas where I can improve as a sergeant major.”

Andrade said one of his key takeaways from CPOI was learning to look to fellow leaders for support.

“The Marine Corps, specifically the infantry, taught me at a young age that you must be able to bear the weight and never pass off your burden, as it takes two guns out of the fight,” said Andrade. “The Chiefs Mess has taught me that the anchor is a heavy burden to hold, but you are never alone. You must be comfortable with asking for help and rely on each other to shoulder the weight.”

Daly hopes completion of CPOI will help strengthen the relationship between the Marines and Sailors throughout Kings Bay and within MCSFBn.

“I hope our junior Marines and Sailors see the strength of the bond we share—different services, but brothers and sisters in the Chiefs Mess,” said Daly. “More importantly, I hope it encourages and inspires everyone across the battalion to look at the bigger picture. At the end of the day, we are all people serving and supporting our country.”

Harris said he appreciates the perspective and standards the Marines brought to this year’s CPOI.

“In my 12 years of CPOI involvement, this year has surpassed all others,” said Harris. “It is no secret that the Marine Corps sets the standard of uncompromising discipline, elite combat readiness, and rigorous physical expectations. The commitment Marines make to defend the nation is matched by an unshakable loyalty to the service member on their left and right. Marines fight for many things—they fight for freedom, for the people beside them, and for the millions they’ll never meet.”

During the pinning ceremony, family members pinned gold fouled anchors on each of the chief selects’ collars, and the CPOI sponsors placed combination covers on their heads.

Daly expressed his gratitude for the opportunity to be accepted into the Chiefs Mess and said he encourages other Marines to participate.

“I’m incredibly proud of the actual chief selects, now chief petty officers in the United States Navy,” said Daly. “I will continue to influence our gunnery sergeants and first sergeants in hopes they’ll face the challenges of chief season to continue to strengthen the bond between the Navy and Marine Corps.”

Though their starting points differed from their Navy counterparts, both Daly and Andrade are now armed with expanded perspectives, fresh leadership tools and a network of support in the Chiefs Mess.

MCSFBn is a joint force of Marines and Sailors that serves as the security force ensuring the protection of strategic assets within the Strategic Weapons Facility Atlantic (SWFLANT) area of responsibility. SWFLANT’s mission is to deliver safe, secure and effective sea-based strategic deterrence capabilities to fleet ballistic missile submarines.

items.title: Software for New F-35 Logistics System Starts Going Live
items.author: Steve Losey
items.summary: The rollout of new hardware to replace an old, troubled maintenance and logistics system for the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter is complete, a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told reporters Sept. 14, and software upgrades are next. The post Software for New F-35 Logistics System Starts Going Live appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .
items.body:
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md. —The effort to replace the F-35’s old, troubled maintenance and logistics system is picking up steam after years of work, a Lockheed Martin spokesperson told reporters Sept. 14, with new computer hardware fielded across the fleet and updated software starting to roll out.

Mireya Villarreal, Lockheed Martin’s spokesperson for the F-35 program, told reporters at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference last week that software upgrades for the Operational Data Integrated Network, or ODIN , have recently begun, and “that transition is going well.”

Sean Jackson, vice president for Lockheed’s F-35 development program, said in a follow-up statement that the ODIN software was installed at Nellis Air Force Base, Nev., in late August. This marked the first operational delivery of ODIN software, he said.

“The new ODIN software takes advantage of capabilities based on recent fleetwide ODIN hardware upgrades to support F-35 fleet operations,” Jackson said. “Lockheed Martin continues to work hand-in-hand with our Air Force partners, aligning the ODIN software upgrade cadence that will cascade new and upgraded capabilities across the fleet.”

ODIN is replacing a previous system called ALIS, for Autonomic Logistics Information System. ALIS was meant to schedule and track F-35 maintenance, keep an eye on which jets were ready to fly, and help the military order spare parts, as well as tracking data in-flight and sending information on how well various systems were performing to maintainers on the ground.

But ALIS was deeply flawed. A 2020 Government Accountability Office report found crucial data that ALIS was supposed to automatically collect was often inaccurate or misleading. This forced maintainers to keep track of that information themselves, sometimes manually entering data in Excel spreadsheets in a time-consuming way.

Its interface was hard to navigate and not user-friendly, and its server units were massive, weighing in at 200 pounds apiece. The entire system weighed nearly 900 pounds and needed a whole room to operate, which officials said made ALIS difficult to deploy or store on a ship.

In 2020, the F-35 Joint Program Office announced Lockheed would design and build ODIN to replace ALIS. Officials say ODIN weighs less than a quarter of the entire ALIS system, has improved computer processing time, and is more secure and easier to service and support. The Pentagon started rolling out new hardware, called ODIN Base Kits, to F-35 squadrons in 2022. The kit can run both the ALIS and ODIN software.

Back in February, the F-35 program office issued a contract modification worth up to $47.7 million to Lockheed for further work on ODIN. Since 2020, the Pentagon has spent $255.1 million under the indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity contract, which has a ceiling of $309.3 million.
