items.title: UK must focus on the Atlantic, ‘foundation’ of Britain’s security: Navy chief
items.author: Rudy Ruitenberg
items.summary: The Royal Navy is spending a growing amount of time and resources to monitor Russian vessels, on average devoting two British warships every week to it.
items.body:
Europe

UK must focus on the Atlantic, ‘foundation’ of Britain’s security: Navy chief

Crew members wave goodbye to family and friends as air-defense destroyer HMS Dragon sets sail from Portsmouth Harbour on March 10, 2026, in Portsmouth, England. (Leon Neal/Getty Images)

PARIS – The United Kingdom must strengthen naval readiness to keep the Atlantic open and protect the sea lanes, undersea cables and energy infrastructure vital to the country, the chief of the Royal Navy said.

Britain faces threats not seen since the Cold War, with Russia increasingly probing the North Atlantic and around critical underwater infrastructure, First Sea Lord Gen. Gwyn Jenkins said in a speech at the historical Admiralty House in central London on Wednesday, with repeated references to the Battle for the Atlantic during World War II.

Jenkins cited the memoirs of Winston Churchill on the significance of the Atlantic, saying the wartime leader understood the sea is not peripheral to Britain but existential. The Atlantic remains central to U.K. security and to NATO’s ability to reinforce Europe, according to the First Sea Lord , who said a “whole-nation effort” is required to defend the sea.

RELATED

NATO allies foil Russian subsea cable sabotage plot

The clandestine Russian operation was carried out by Moscow’s GUGI undersea warfare directorate to test a destructive sabotage capability, sources said.

“We must know what is happening in the Atlantic, protect what matters, keep open the sea lanes, and convince any adversary that the cost of coercion or aggression would outweigh any possible gain,” Jenkins said, according to a transcript of the speech. “If we are to prevail in the Atlantic again, we must strengthen our warfighting readiness and rediscover what it means to be a maritime nation.”

The First Sea Lord said British dependence on the Atlantic has grown in the past 80 years, with almost all of the U.K.’s trade moving by sea, and almost all its energy, food, raw materials and exports flowing via maritime routes. He noted a “dangerous paradox,” saying that while the Atlantic has arguably never mattered more to the country, the sea is increasingly invisible in the public’s mind.

Control of the Atlantic has always been closely linked to control of its northern approaches, the Navy chief said, citing the defeat of Norway during World War II that allowed the Nazis to threaten allied shipping lanes, and the importance of the Greenland-Iceland-UK gap during the Cold War.

The Norwegian Sea, the Arctic and the northern approaches are not distant theaters but “form our open sea border with Russia,” according to Jenkins, who said the Joint Expeditionary Force is increasingly important there. The U.K.-led military alliance includes the five Nordic countries, the three Baltic states as well as the Netherlands.

Jenkins said the ten JEF countries will finalize a “Northern Navies” agreement this year to move beyond what he called episodic activity and to create a persistent, integrated maritime force, in response to the security threat presented by Russia.

Russia has advanced submarines that are increasingly difficult to track, long-range precision weapons and specialist deep-water systems, and is “probing, testing and mapping,” Jenkins said. The Royal Navy is spending a growing amount of time and resources to monitor Russian vessels, on average deploying two British warships every week for that purpose, according to the navy chief.

The First Sea Lord defended plans to create a “hybrid Navy,” saying future advantage will come from integrated networks linking crewed vessels, drones, sensors and data. He said that while there are skeptics, the concept is not optional.

“It is no longer possible to defend a vast, contested ocean with crewed warships alone,” Jenkins said. “A ship operating alone is now vulnerable. But a ship commanding a network of large uncrewed escorts, drones and autonomous sensors, that is a different proposition. That’s why we must blend old and new, crewed and uncrewed.”

Rudy Ruitenberg is a Europe correspondent for Defense News. He started his career at Bloomberg News and has experience reporting on technology, commodity markets and politics.

items.title: Preserving Jobs and Tax Revenue in the Age of AI: Q&A with Carter Price
items.summary: Carter Price, a mathematician at RAND and co-director of the RAND Von Furstenberg Family Budget Model Initiative, discusses ways to rebalance the tax code so that it doesn't incentivize employers to replace humans with AI.
items.body:
Preserving Jobs and Tax Revenue in the Age of AI: Q&A with Carter Price

Commentary

Sep 17, 2026

If AI starts to replace jobs, it isn't just American workers who will feel the loss of income. So will the U.S. Treasury.

Nearly two-thirds of all federal revenue comes from taxes levied on human labor, a recent RAND study noted. That revenue will not be easy to make up if AI starts to put large numbers of people out of work.

Carter Price has been looking for ways to rebalance the tax code so that it doesn't incentivize employers to replace humans with AI. He's a mathematician at RAND and co-director of the RAND Von Furstenberg Family Budget Model Initiative . And he has an idea for how to give workers an edge in the age of AI.

How does the existing tax code disincentivize keeping human workers on the job?

We went through all 7,000 pages of the tax code with a tool we built as part of the RAND Budget Model Initiative. It allows us to identify every provision, every line item, and its implications. There's a lot in there. But we identified several places where the existing U.S tax code works against companies hiring or keeping workers.

The employer payroll tax is one obvious example. Companies have to pay that tax for every worker they hire, so more workers means more expense. Meanwhile, the tax code allows companies to write off the depreciation of big, expensive assets early, before those assets actually wear out. That can make buying something like a robotic system much more cost-effective—which makes that tax write-off a direct subsidy for displacing human workers.

What's your idea to change the incentives here?

You and I pay progressive taxes on our income. That means if we make more money, we move into a higher tax bracket.

Our idea is somewhat similar, but for companies. The government would tax high corporate profits per worker in addition to taxing their income overall.

Imagine a company makes $1 million in profit and has 100 employees. Its profit per worker is $10,000. Now let's say that company brings in a lot of AI and lays off all but ten of its workers. Now its profit per worker is $100,000, and it just moved into a higher tax bracket. It's going to pay more in taxes for that same $1 million in profit.

AI might still be so much more efficient that it still makes sense for some companies to replace those workers. This tax structure wouldn't stand in the way of that.

But where the current tax code sometimes disincentivizes keeping human workers, our proposed change would flip the script. It would put the tax code more on the side of workers instead of on the side of AI and automation.

What else did your tax code analysis find that could help promote employment?

We found a lot of special, niche provisions that are just scattered throughout the tax code. You could eliminate those and really clean everything up. There are three different clean-energy vehicle tax provisions, for example, and they all do pretty much the same thing.

These niche provisions pointed us to a suite of changes that could really make a difference. The government could eliminate those special tax breaks. That would bring in additional revenue.

The federal government could then eliminate the employer payroll tax and replace it with two business taxes: one a flat tax on business revenue, and the other the per-worker tax on high profits.

Companies would be no worse off. The government would balance the loss of revenue from eliminating the payroll tax with an increase from eliminating special tax carve-outs. And we'd be incentivizing human employment instead of using tax breaks to incentivize things like investments in distilled spirits.

Our proposed change would put the tax code more on the side of workers instead of on the side of AI and automation.

What would it take to implement those changes?

It takes an act of Congress to change the Internal Revenue Code. But that's a low barrier compared to what some other popular policy ideas that are floating around would face. For example, a value-added tax, which would be like a nationwide sales tax, would require an entirely new tax-collection infrastructure. And a federal wealth tax, which could generate revenue from huge concentrations of wealth, would require a constitutional amendment in addition to new tax-collection infrastructure.

By contrast, policymakers could at least theoretically wake up tomorrow and pass a law that would make the tax code more robust by reducing its dependence on income from labor.

Furthermore, simplifying the tax code would give people back millions of hours that they currently spend filling out forms. It would improve the efficiency of the economy, and that's something everyone can like.

What motivates you to do this work?

I'm a mathematician. And there have been a lot of headlines about the advances that AI models have made in mathematics in particular. AI can generate code that would take a human hours, or even days, to write. I'm biased, but I think human mathematicians still provide a lot of value that AI can't fully replace. I'm not sure that will be true forever. But until that changes, we shouldn't rush into replacing workers with AI, and our tax code certainly shouldn't incentivize employers to do so.

The regulated community should use the MAA request for change ( RFC ) form to submit a proposal for change to regulatory articles ( RA ’s) or associated manuals.

To request clarification of regulation meaning, routine correspondence methods such as email, letter and telephone may be used.

The MAA may still request a completed MAA RFC form, depending on the nature of the enquiry.

Notwithstanding that formal amendment may result from a clarification request, initial requests for clarification should not be submitted on a MAA RFC form.

The MAA RFC form can be submitted via email to the MAA regulatory publications team ( MRPT ) at dsa-maa-mrp enquires . If clarification is required regarding the need for submission of an MAA RFC form, then the regulated community can contact the MRPT .

items.title: Germany sending fighter jets to Latvia to protect election from drone incidents
items.author: Linus Höller
items.summary: Germany will send four Eurofighter jets to defend Latvian airspace during upcoming elections, amid concerns over drone incursions from Russia and Belarus.
items.body:
Europe

Germany sending fighter jets to Latvia to protect election from drone incidents

An Eurofighter aircraft of the German Air Force sits on the tarmac at the Latvian air base of Lielvarde in April 2024. (Alexander Welscher/picture alliance via Getty Images)

VIENNA — Germany will send four Eurofighter jets to defend Latvian airspace during its upcoming elections, as concerns over drone incursions from neighboring Russia and Belarus remain high.

Berlin plans to dispatch four Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jets, alongside a contingent of several dozen soldiers and technicians, to the Lielvārde air base in central Latvia. They will be there for a week in late September and early October, the German ministry of defense said in a statement.

Latvian authorities had requested support from allies to secure the skies over the country during the general election, Germany said. The Latvian parliamentary election is scheduled to take place Oct. 3.

The mission is billed as part of NATO’s enhanced air policing north, or eAPN, in the Baltic States, though the short, one-week timeline and narrower election focus set it apart from the alliance’s routine four-month rotations.

None of the three small Baltic States possess their own fighter aircraft. Unlike northern Estonia and southern Lithuania, Latvia is not usually home to permanently stationed NATO jets; instead, the allied aircraft stationed in the neighboring states also cover Latvian skies.

The Baltic states in particular have been calling for strong NATO commitments to secure the alliance’s eastern flank, as governments in the three small countries feel particularly threatened by Russia. This year, repeated unauthorized drone incursions have additionally put the countries on edge. Some of these have been identified as Ukrainian drones that strayed off course from their targets in Russia, while other instances remain unidentified.

Significantly, Italian NATO jets in neighboring Lithuania shot down a suspected Russian-made drone this week after it crossed the border from Belarus. It was the first time a drone was shot down in Lithuanian airspace.

Lielvārde air base, where the German Eurofighters will be stationed during their mission, has also seen rotating contingents of other NATO countries’ fighter jets. Just a few weeks ago, in late August, two Turkish F-16 fighter jets visited the base. In April, French Rafale jets based out of Šiauliai, Lithuania, visited the airfield. NATO has also used the base for its AWACS aircraft during missions along the Russian border.

Latvia and its two Baltic neighbors have been members of NATO since 2004, joining alongside fellow eastern flank countries Slovakia, Romania and Bulgaria, and Slovenia.

Linus Höller is Defense News' Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

items.title: India says China has scaled back troop numbers along their border
items.author: Anjana Pasricha
items.summary: Both countries had amassed tens of thousands of troops along their poorly demarcated Himalayan border following a deadly clash in 2020.
items.body:
Asia Pacific

India says China has scaled back troop numbers along their border

This video frame grab taken from footage recorded in mid-June 2020 and released by China Central Television (CCTV) on Feb. 20, 2021, shows Indian soldiers crossing a river during an incident where Chinese and Indian troops clashed in the Line of Actual Control (LAC) in the Galwan Valley, in the Karakoram Mountains in the Himalayas. (CCTV/AFP via Getty Images)

NEW DELHI — India’s Defense Ministry said that China significantly reduced troop deployment along the border with India in 2025 as increased political, diplomatic and military engagement helped ease tensions between the two Asian powers.

Both countries had amassed tens of thousands of troops along their poorly demarcated Himalayan border following a deadly clash in 2020.

“The year 2025 witnessed significant reduction in deployment of People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Force opposite Northern Borders, with 10 Combined Arms Brigade size forces each deployed in areas along the LAC and in traditional training areas,” the Defense Ministry stated in its annual report for 2025-26 released Monday.

The LAC or Line of Actual Control refers to the roughly 3,500 kilometers long Indo-Chinese frontier in the Himalayas. Much of the boundary remains disputed.

The report said that bilateral interactions at political, diplomatic and military levels had facilitated “positive developments along the northern border, leading to stability.”

However the Defense Ministry did not provide figures for Indian troop deployments along the Indo-Chinese border but said that the Indian Army’s deployment “in all sectors” along the LAC remained “robust, well poised, and prepared to deal with any emerging contingency.”

The report also highlighted India’s accelerated construction of tunnels, roads and other all-weather infrastructure in the Himalayas, which it said is critical for the rapid movement of troops, equipment and supplies.

Analysts point out that China has similarly expanded infrastructure on its side of the border in recent years, suggesting that even as troop deployment eases, long-term military readiness remains a priority for both sides along their border.

“Maintaining a strong dissuasive posture and preparedness along the borders is an imperative. We cannot scale down our defenses irrespective of troop numbers,” said retired Brigadier Arun Sahgal, who directs the Forum for Strategic Initiatives in New Delhi.

The report comes amid a broader thaw in India-China relations. Chinese President Xi Jinping visited New Delhi for the annual BRICS summit last week, his first trip to India in seven years. The visit marked another step in efforts by the two countries to stabilize relations after years of tensions triggered by the 2020 border clash.

After a meeting between the two leaders on the sidelines of the summit, Xi said China viewed India-China relations from a “strategic and long-term perspective” and called on the two countries to support one another and pursue common development. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said peace and tranquility along the disputed border were essential to the continued development of bilateral ties.

India’s foreign ministry said that “the two leaders expressed commitment to a fair, reasonable and mutually acceptable resolution of the boundary question.”

Tensions between India and China began to ease after Xi and Modi met in Russia in October 2024 leading to an agreement that helped end the military standoff in eastern Ladakh.

items.title: Guidance: Spousal employment - Supplementary Agreement Germany
items.summary: The NATO Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) and the Supplementary Agreement are the international legal agreements that enable UK Defence to operate in Germany.
items.body:
The NATO SOFA is a multinational agreement between nations enabling the operation of a nation’s defence task in the territory of another nation.

In Germany, the stationing and operation of UK Defence personnel is governed by the Supplementary Agreement to the NATO SOFA. The Supplementary Agreement expands upon the provisions of the NATO SOFA and forms part of German domestic law, providing the detailed legal framework under which UK Defence operates in Germany.

Overview

Neither the NATO SOFA nor the Supplementary Agreement provides a direct legal entitlement for accompanying spouses or family members to undertake employment in Germany.

The agreements provide a basis for lawful residence and status in Germany for eligible dependants accompanying members of the force or civilian component. Any employment activity undertaken by a dependant must, however, comply with applicable German law.

The UK Ministry of Defence cannot grant authority, permission, or exemptions allowing spouses or dependants to work in Germany. Responsibility for ensuring compliance with host nation legislation rests with the individual and, where applicable, their employer.

There are several routes through which accompanying spouses may lawfully undertake employment within Germany, subject to the relevant legal and regulatory requirements.

Employment within the German Economy

The status of an accompanying spouse is recognised under German immigration arrangements associated with the Supplementary Agreement and NATO SOFA framework. Consequently, accompanying spouses generally do not require a separate residence permit or work permit to seek employment in the German economy.

Individuals employed by German or other locally established employers will be subject to German legislation and jurisdiction. This may include:

employment law

taxation requirements

social security contributions

health insurance obligations

pension arrangements

other statutory and regulatory requirements

The decision to undertake employment within the German economy is a personal one. Individuals are responsible for ensuring that their employment arrangements comply fully with German law.

Neither the Supplementary Agreement nor the NATO SOFA provides exemptions from German employment, tax, social security, healthcare, or other legal obligations arising from employment.

Operating a Business or Undertaking Self-Employment in Germany

Accompanying spouses may be able to establish and operate a business, trade, profession, or other self-employed activity within the Federal Republic of Germany, subject to the relevant approvals, registrations, and regulatory requirements imposed by the German authorities.

Any business activity undertaken for commercial gain and participating in the German economy will ordinarily be subject to applicable German legislation. This may include taxation, social security obligations, health insurance requirements, licensing provisions, and other regulatory controls.

Individuals considering self-employment or the operation of a business should seek appropriate professional advice from qualified German legal, tax, and financial advisers before commencing any activity.

Care should be taken to maintain a clear distinction between any commercial activity and the rights, privileges, or status derived from dependant status under the NATO SOFA and Supplementary Agreement.

International remote working (IRW)

Neither the NATO SOFA nor the Supplementary Agreement establishes a legal framework for International Remote Working (IRW).

Remote working arrangements are a matter between the employee and their employer. The UK MOD cannot authorise or validate remote working arrangements undertaken within the territory of another sovereign state. This includes those attracting the term Crown Servant (Civil or Military) not assigned to Germany for the purpose of their employment.

Before commencing any form of remote working from Germany, both the employee and employer should satisfy themselves that the arrangement is lawful and compliant with all relevant German legal requirements.

Consideration should be given to matters including:

employment legislation

taxation obligations

social security requirements

healthcare obligations

health and safety legislation

data protection and privacy regulations

any other relevant regulatory requirements

Depending on the circumstances, German law may impose obligations on either the employee or employer, even where the employer is established outside Germany and the work is undertaken remotely.

Employees and employers are strongly encouraged to seek independent legal and professional advice from appropriately qualified German advisers before commencing any remote working arrangement.

Where the work involves access to official, government, or sensitive information, additional security considerations may apply. Individuals should ensure compliance with all relevant departmental security policies and seek advice from their employing organisation where necessary.

Key Principles

The Supplementary Agreement and NATO SOFA do not provide a right to employment for accompanying spouses.

Any employment, self-employment, or business activity in Germany must comply with German law.

The MOD cannot grant permission or exemptions for employment activities in Germany.

International Remote Working is not covered by the Supplementary Agreement or NATO SOFA.

Individuals and employers are responsible for ensuring that any employment arrangement is lawful and compliant with applicable host nation requirements.

items.title: Japanese Global Hawk drone splashes down in crash
items.author: Gordon Arthur
items.summary: A Japanese Global Hawk drone nosedived into the Sea of Japan this week, instantly slashing the country’s fleet of these drones by a third.
items.body:
Asia Pacific

Japanese Global Hawk drone splashes down in crash

This picture taken on Jan. 23, 2023, shows a Global Hawk unmanned surveillance aircraft of the Japan Air Self-Defence Force (JASDF) in Misawa, Aomori prefecture. (Jiji Press / AFP via Getty Images)

CHRISTCHURCH, New Zealand — A Japanese Global Hawk drone nosedived into the Sea of Japan on Sept. 15, instantly slashing the country’s fleet of these large-wingspan, unmanned surveillance aircraft by a third.

Japan paid roughly $163 million for Northrop Grumman to manufacture each of its three RQ-4B Block 30i Global Hawks nearly a decade ago.

The Japan Air Self-Defense Force (JASDF) on Sept. 16 revealed that it lost contact with the high-altitude drone at 12:55 p.m., before losing its radar signature three minutes later over international waters.

The JASDF’s 502nd Squadron operates its Global Hawks from Misawa Air Base in northern Japan. Before crashing, the drone had taken off at 10.20 a.m. on an unspecified mission, with JASDF Chief of Staff Gen. Takehiro Morita only divulging, “This particular flight was not a training exercise.”

One mission for Japanese Global Hawks, which can stay aloft for 32 hours at altitudes of up to 60,000 ft, is monitoring North Korean missile launch preparations. They are also useful for keeping an eye on Chinese military activities.

Morita said a Japan Coast Guard helicopter spotted debris in the water just 50 minutes after it had lost contact. Other assets spotted further wreckage and took photos, enabling precise identification of the aircraft.

No cause of the accident was revealed.

Japan received its first Global Hawk in March 2022, with the other two arriving later that year. Their integrated payload contains an electro-optic/infrared sensor, synthetic aperture radar and ground moving target indicator.

The Global Hawk purchase was controversial in Japan given their enormous cost and the fact that the U.S. retained tight control over the aircraft’s technology and the processing of gathered data.

Global Hawks possess the longest reach of any Japanese drone, so the loss of one among such a small fleet will be sorely missed.

However, as Japan increasingly prioritizes unmanned technologies, the Japan Maritime Self Defense Force is planning to induct the first of 23 MQ-9B SeaGuardians in 2027. Although these drones have a shorter endurance and range than the Global Hawk, Tokyo will use them for maritime domain awareness.

Japan’s draft 2027 defense budget requested US$1.88 billion for the first 17 SeaGuardians. These will take over some of the missions currently performed by P-1 and older P-3C Orion maritime patrol aircraft.

Incidentally, the U.S. Air Force currently has three RQ-4B Global Hawks stationed at Yokota Air Base in Tokyo, after relocating them from Guam in May to avoid the typhoon season.

The United States planned to quickly retire all its Global Hawks, but it will now keep operating them until 2033. After that, there will be only three in South Korea and two in Japan still flying.

Gordon Arthur is an Asia correspondent for Defense News. After a 20-year stint working in Hong Kong, he now resides in New Zealand. He has attended military exercises and defense exhibitions in about 20 countries around the Asia-Pacific region.

Details

The Germany Enabling Office (GEO) is the United Kingdom’s military mission in Germany and the responsible authority for enabling, monitoring and assuring the conduct of United Kingdom defence in Germany under the United Kingdom’s obligations to the NATO Status of Forces Agreement (NATO SOFA) and the Supplementary Agreement (SA) in Germany.

The NATO SOFA and the SA are the international legal agreements enabling the military of the United Kingdom to operate in Germany.

Our engagement with UK defence personnel in Germany, and where applicable broader Europe, is routinely through the customer-facing UK National Support Elements (UK NSE).

Though the GEO is not directly customer facing you will receive communication from us via your NSE. Our routine official communications with those NSE are in the form of information notes.

Where possible those information notes will be made available on this webpage.

items.title: Battle for the Atlantic
items.summary: First Sea Lord and Chief of the Naval Staff General Sir Gwyn Jenkins delivered a speech at Admiralty House, Department of Naval Research.
items.body:
Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen.

Thank you for joining us, and my thanks to the Department for Naval Research for organising today’s symposium.

As we gather here at Admiralty House, the importance of sea power will not be lost on any of you.

That is because our history has been shaped by the sea.

Because our prosperity, security and influence have for centuries depended on our ability to master it, protect what moves across it, and deny its advantages to those who threaten us.

That’s why my speech today is focused on the Atlantic.

Not simply as a vast body of water, or a theatre of past conflict, but as a foundation of Britain’s security.

Eighty years ago, Britain and her allies fought the longest campaign of the Second World War at sea.

It was fought by sailors, merchant seamen, aircrew, dockyard workers, engineers, scientists and codebreakers…

By men and women who kept Britain alive as Europe fell under Nazi occupation.

Convoys crossed a hostile ocean in atrocious weather, under air attack and constant U-boat threat.

They carried the food, fuel, raw materials, weapons and reinforcements on which our national survival depended.

In 1941, Churchill named this struggle the Battle of the Atlantic.

It was the prospect of losing this Battle – not the Blitz, not the threat to the Empire in the East – that truly frightened him.

As Churchill observed later in his memoirs, Britain’s ability to “carry on the war, or even keep ourselves alive,” rested fundamentally “on our mastery of the ocean routes and the free approach and entry to our ports.”

Churchill attached such significance to the Atlantic because he understood something important.

The sea is not peripheral to Britain – it is existential.

If those maritime arteries had been severed during the War…

Had Britain lost the Atlantic…

Our life support would have been switched off.

We would have struggled to cling on before the Americans joined the fight…

Europe would not have been liberated…

And victory would have been impossible.

That does not diminish the role of our other services, whose contribution to the war was also vital.

Yesterday, we marked the 86th anniversary of the Battle of Britain, a campaign that denied the Luftwaffe air superiority and was also integral to our survival.

And as the son of an RAF crypto mechanic, I know how important air power was and remains to our nation.

But the point I am making is this:

Without the Royal Navy and the RAF, who is to say whether Hitler would have abandoned Operation Sealion and switched his focus to invading Russia instead.

Who is to say whether the Army would have been able to campaign in North Africa, the Med or in mainland Europe.

Sea power not only sustained us during the War.

It arguably saved us.

Lose the war at sea and you lose the war.

That was the warning of Admiral Pound, the First Sea Lord of the day – and it remains true now.

If we are to prevail in the Atlantic again, we must strengthen our warfighting readiness and rediscover what it means to be a maritime nation.

Not because history repeats itself perfectly.

It doesn’t.

But because the factors that made the Atlantic decisive eighty years ago remain decisive today.

The world may have changed beyond recognition – but our dependence on the Atlantic has only grown since.

Almost all our trade moves by sea, and America remains by far our biggest trading partner.

Almost all our energy, food, raw materials and exports flow through maritime routes.

Beneath the waves, our nuclear deterrent protects the nation.

Undersea cables carry almost all data, transactions, and communications on which modern life depends.

In all these areas, the Atlantic is critical.

During the war, the British people understood that a submarine attack on an allied convoy hundreds of miles away had direct consequences at home.

But today, we have reached a dangerous paradox…

The sea, the Atlantic, has arguably never mattered more to Britain.

We are certainly much more reliant on it than we were in the 1930s.

And yet it has become increasingly invisible in the public’s mind.

Supermarket shelves are filled, homes are heated, money moves instantly and the internet turbocharges our modern lives.

We have made this huge progress seem effortless.

But it was not effortless.

It was earned. It was fought for. We have continuously defended it.

And if that defence fails, the consequences will be felt quickly in every household, every business and every department of state.

Our adversaries understand that.

They understand our dependence on the sea and the seabed.

They understand that the Atlantic is not empty space.

It is strategic terrain: the bridge between North America, Europe and with the world.

The route through which NATO reinforcement would move.

The space through which our trade, energy, data and deterrence are sustained.

That is why the lessons of the War remain so important.

In the 1940s, the question was whether Britain could stay connected to the industrial, economic and military strength of North America and its Empire.

Today, in an age of missiles, cyber, space surveillance, and rapid technological change, we also face added challenges, because the seabed has become a new arena of contest.

Uncrewed systems are changing how we fight, advancing at a rate many nations are struggling to keep pace with.

Information is moving faster than it has ever moved before.

And yet, many of the fundamentals remain the same.

The Atlantic is the same body of water…

We are still an island…

We still rely on it to move the goods, fuel and commodities we rely on…

And our most important alliances are still trans-Atlantic.

That is why this issue reaches beyond uniform.

The Atlantic is a military, industrial, diplomatic and economic challenge – and an opportunity.

That is why we need a whole-nation effort if we are to continue to defend it.

History shows us this.

The original Battle of the Atlantic was not won by one decisive action.

It was won by cumulative advantage: better intelligence, faster shipbuilding, improved tactics, effective air cover, convoy discipline and a willingness to learn under pressure.

It was won by leadership, the spirit to fight and the urge to win.

The same approach is required today, but with different tools and in a different context.

We should not allow the complexity of modern technology to muddy what is a simple task.

We must know what is happening in the Atlantic, protect what matters, keep open the sea lanes, and convince any adversary that the cost of coercion or aggression would outweigh any possible gain.

That is the test of warfighting readiness.

Can we fight tonight? Can we sustain the fight tomorrow? And can we adapt faster than our adversaries?

That is the standard by which the Navy must be judged.

The Battle of the Atlantic demonstrated another enduring lesson.

There is only one thing worse than fighting with allies, and that is fighting without them.

No nation secured the Atlantic alone in the 1940s, and no nation will do so now.

Victory depended on Allied integration: navies, merchant fleets, air forces, intelligence, scientists and industry working to a common purpose.

That same principle underpins NATO today.

In any major crisis, NATO’s ability to reinforce Europe depends upon secure access across the Atlantic.

It remains central to collective defence.

That is why the Royal Navy’s role in the Atlantic cannot be separated from NATO’s wider mission.

Our task is to contribute to collective deterrence, support the movement of Allied forces, protect critical infrastructure, maintain awareness and ensure freedom of manoeuvre.

This is also why partnerships matter.

Whether through NATO, bilateral relationships or the Joint Expeditionary Force, our security is strengthened when we operate alongside allies who share our interests and values.

For the United Kingdom, this is both a responsibility and an opportunity.

We are a nuclear power, a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, a founding member of NATO and the framework nation for the JEF.

We are still one of the most powerful navies in the world.

Our geography, history and alliances give us both a particular stake in the North Atlantic and the ability to act with others at scale.

Which leads me onto the third lesson of the War: our northern flank matters.

The Atlantic cannot be understood without understanding the High North, because control of the ocean has always been closely linked to control of its northern approaches.

The consequences of losing control were painfully evident in 1940, when Norway’s defeat gave the Nazis control of the coastline and deep-water fjords from which they were able to threaten allied shipping lanes in the Atlantic.

Later, the Greenland-Iceland-UK Gap became integral in the Cold War.

And today, its relevance remains undiminished.

The Norwegian Sea, the Arctic and the northern approaches are not distant theatres.

They are the gateway to our backyard; they form our open sea border with Russia.

They are where British security, NATO and European stability come together.

And it is also where the JEF makes an increasingly important contribution.

For more than a decade, the UK has led ten like-minded nations that are able to respond quickly to threats in the High North, North Atlantic and Baltic.

It complements NATO, but it also gives us the speed, political alignment and geographic focus to seize the initiative early.

As First Sea Lord, I have been determined to make that partnership stronger.

That is why we have been working with the JEF members on a new Northern Navies agreement, which we will finalise this year.

It will move us beyond episodic activity to a persistent, integrated maritime force.

Navies that train together, exercise together, plan together and, if necessary, fight together.

It requires common systems, shared digital networks, common doctrine, shared logistics and stockpiles…

This isn’t just about fighting together. It’s about building a common British and Norwegian frigate force.

It’s about ensuring a Danish frigate can seamlessly takeover from a British warship in the Atlantic, while also taking control of our flotilla of uncrewed ships and sensors that will remain in position for months on end.

This is how we turn collective strength into credible deterrence.

This is how we create a Vanguard for NATO.

A family of Northern Navies, led by the UK, stronger than the sum of its parts.

Making the Hybrid Navy real, with allies.

The reason why we need this is simple: the greatest threat to our security today is Russia.

That threat is felt most acutely in the maritime domain – in the North Atlantic, in the High North.

Russia retains advanced submarines that are increasingly difficult to track, long-range precision weapons, and specialist systems designed to operate deep underwater.

It is increasingly active in our domain, and we are spending increasing amounts of time and resource monitoring Russian vessels and the shadow fleet.

On average, two Royal Navy warships are now being deployed every week for this purpose.

Russia is probing, testing, and mapping.

It seeks advantage in the grey zone, particularly around the critical undersea infrastructure on which modern societies rely.

And among Ukraine’s western allies, Russia considers us to be one of its greatest foes.

We know that Russia is probing us for weakness.

And we are facing threats…in a way we have not been since the Cold War.

That does not mean we are returning to the days before the Berlin Wall fell.

Nor am I saying that war is inevitable. There are strong parallels, but this is not the 1930s.

The circumstances are different, the technologies have changed, and the context is more complex.

But many of the underlying challenges remain.

That is why the Royal Navy continues to invest in anti-submarine warfare, underwater surveillance, maritime aviation and Allied integration.

This is why we are building the Hybrid Navy.

This is not about seeking confrontation.

It is about preventing it through credible capability, strong alliances, presence and the ability to respond immediately when required.

During the Second World War, German U-boats sought to isolate Britain by attacking the merchant shipping.

Today, the form of the threat is different, but the significance of the underwater domain has grown rather than diminished.

Critical undersea infrastructure is now part of the strategic landscape. Cables, pipelines, sensors and energy networks connect nations, markets and command systems.

They are difficult to monitor, hard to repair at speed and increasingly integral to national resilience.

The day that the UK declared war on Germany, the allies severed its transatlantic telegraph cables.

I pray it does not happen, but were we to go to war again, we know our enemies will try to use the same playbook against us.

That is why protection of the High North, the Atlantic, and of our underwater CNI is not just about naval capability.

It also rests on intelligence, industry, law enforcement, commercial partnerships and close allied coordination.

It is a national endeavour.

The Royal Marines Commandos also play a crucial role in that effort.

The Atlantic campaign was never fought at sea alone.

Its outcome depended upon control of key geography around the wider Atlantic basin, and that lesson remains directly relevant to the northern flank today.

The ability to monitor, secure and influence activity across the maritime domain requires more than ships and submarines.

It requires forces able to operate where sea and land intersect, to work with allies in difficult terrain, and to create advantage before a crisis becomes a conflict.

That is where the Commandos make a uniquely important contribution.

Tough, resilient and resourceful, honed for some of the toughest environments on the planet, they are the tip of the spear when it comes to NATO’s strike forces.

And it is through them that we help create conditions for maritime operations to succeed.

The strategic logic would be familiar to the Commandos of the Second World War.

In May 1940, the Royal Marines led the pre-emptive occupation of Iceland, denying Germany a potential Atlantic base and enabling Allied ships and aircraft to support the convoys.

At St Nazaire, in March 1942, Commandos destroyed the dry dock that could have supported Tirpitz and other German warships raiding those convoys.

And months later, Royal Marines paddled by night into occupied Bordeaux during Operation Frankton, damaging vital Axis shipping and disrupting the blockade runners that sustained Germany’s war effort.

Today, the Commando Force may have undergone a generational transformation – but it remains just as important to our success.

The Royal Marines are part of an integrated fighting system. They have also evolved over the past decade because modern warfare demands adaptation.

The more we integrate, the more we adapt, the greater our advantage over our adversaries.

That logic also sits at the heart of the most radical and far-reaching reform we are undertaking currently: the move to a Hybrid Navy.

The maritime battlespace is becoming increasingly distributed, connected and data-driven.

Our future advantage will come from integrated networks combining ships, submarines, aircraft, autonomous systems, sensors, data and people.

Ukraine has shown how quickly maritime warfare can change.

In the Black Sea, uncrewed systems and long-range strikes have destroyed a Russian fleet that once seemed dominant.

In the Gulf and the Red Sea, drones and missiles have shown how quickly global trade can be disrupted.

The lesson is not that traditional platforms no longer matter.

It is that it is no longer possible to defend a vast, contested ocean with crewed warships alone.

A ship operating alone is now vulnerable.

But a ship commanding a network of large uncrewed escorts, drones and autonomous sensors…that is a different proposition.

That’s why we must blend old and new. Crewed and uncrewed.

We need a connected fighting force.

This is about changing how we generate combat power.

It will make the Fleet bigger, more lethal, harder to target and knock out of the fight, while also allowing us to adapt faster and impose more dilemma on the enemy.

That is the Hybrid Navy in a nutshell.

Unsurprisingly, we are shaping it around the Atlantic…

Through our Atlantic Series…

Atlantic Bastion is about defending the UK’s continuous at sea deterrent and the critical national infrastructure on which our country, economy and allies depend.

It is the creation of a defensive net across the North Atlantic: crewed and uncrewed ships, drones, sensors, artificial intelligence and weapons working above, on and below the sea to detect, deter and, if necessary, neutralise hostile activity.

Atlantic Shield is about protecting the homeland, the Fleet and our allies from drones, hypersonic weapons and ballistic threats through modern air and missile defence.

And Atlantic Strike is about giving us the ability to hit harder, from greater distance, if an adversary attacks us.

These are the practical building blocks of a new way of fighting.

A new Atlantic Fleet.

The objective is clear: to create a force that can detect threats earlier, respond faster, strike more precisely, survive in the most contested conditions and integrate better with allies.

Yes it is radical, yes we are early adopters, and yes there are sceptics.

But let me be clear: the Hybrid Navy is not opional.

And nor is the need to change our relationship with industry.

During the War we did not just outfight Nazi Germany; we innovated faster and built ships and aircraft at a pace the Reich simply could not match.

The same must be true again now if we are to prevail.

That means we have to move at the speed of the threat.

Software can change a system overnight. Commercial technology can reach the battlefield in days. Our procurement, testing and adoption cycles must reflect that reality.

That means more experimentation, more courage to fail quickly, and the ability to scale what works.

Yes, that creates more risk.

But as First Sea Lord, the only risk that really keeps me up at night is being asked to go to war – and losing.

That is the one risk I will not accept – because my job is not to lose.

My job is to win.

So, as we look to the future, what more must we do?

First, we must not lose focus on the here and now.

We must keep the Atlantic open.

We must continue to protect shipping, reinforcement routes, subsea cables, energy infrastructure and the deterrent.

We are recapitalising the entire nuclear enterprise for the first time since its creation.

We are growing the fleet, with 13 new frigates..

Six command ships for the Hybrid Navy…

Fleet solid support ships…

Four amphibious transport ships for our Commandos…

Two new Astute-class boats, four new Dreadnought-class submarines, and up to 12 next generations SSNs.

We have a Defence Investment Plan, unlocking our uncrewed systems and the Atlantic Series.

But there are plenty of obstacles that risk slowing us down.

We must be relentless in identifying and removing them.

Second, we must invest in people.

Technology changes the character of warfare, but it does not win wars.

Our people remain decisive – and it is leadership, leadership excellence, that wins wars.

War will always remain a contest of human will. That is why we must equip our people with the skills and leadership tools to enable them to win at all levels.

They will have to command distributed forces, fight with uncrewed systems, and make decisions under pressure.

Third, we must act with urgency.

The generation that won the Battle of the Atlantic did so because they learned faster than the enemy.

We are seeing Ukraine do this right now on the front line – and we must do the same.

Perhaps most importantly of all, we must reconnect with the public.

The Battle of the Atlantic still resonates because people understood the connection between events at sea and the war writ large.

We are a maritime nation, an Island Nation – and it’s time we remembered it.

We should make that case with confidence, because many of the qualities that made Britain a maritime power remain.

London is still the global hub of maritime services, insurance, law and finance.

British expertise still shapes the rules and contracts on which global trade depends.

And our ports, shipyards and maritime businesses remain part of an ecosystem that few countries can match.

From the frigates being built on the Clyde and at Rosyth…

To the new Dreadnought submarines at Barrow…

The fleet support at Birkenhead…

Marine engineering at Tyne and Wear and advanced manufacturing in Cumbria…

Investment in the maritime is helping fuel our northern powerhouse.

Across the country, we have a thriving maritime sector worth £224 billion to the UK economy.

It supports 1.7 million jobs and 8,000 businesses….

And that’s before you consider the untapped potential.

That is why we must also reject any idea that the only future for the Royal Navy is one of decline.

Of course, the United States and China operate at a scale others cannot match.

But that does not mean Britain should lower its sights.

We can still be the greatest naval power in Europe, and one of the world’s most powerful navies.

We should not forget just how important our capabilities are, nor the influence and credibility that gives us among our allies.

From aircraft carriers to F35s…

To SSBNs and SSNs…

From frigates and destroyers to the Royal Marines.

Through the Hybrid Navy, we also have a chance to lead the global maritime autonomy race, creating military advantage while generating new economic growth.

We must match this with a serious shipbuilding strategy: ships built in Britain, for us, and exported from Britain, for our allies.

That must surely be the vision: a stronger Navy, a stronger economy, and a stronger maritime nation.

The Battle of the Atlantic was a battle for survival.

It proved that Britain’s ability to determine its own future depended on our naval power, on our ability to remain connected to the wider world.

That lesson endures.

The threat has evolved, the High North has regained strategic prominence, and the seabed has become contested.

New vulnerabilities have emerged, and so have new opportunities.

But one truth remains constant: we depend on the sea.

The Royal Navy’s task is to ensure that, with our allies, with industry, and with the whole maritime nation behind us, Britain is ready.

Ready to lead. Ready to fight. Ready to win.

The Battle of the Atlantic is one of the most important chapters in our history.

And when our own history is written, I am certain the Atlantic will prove decisive once again.

Thank you.

items.title: Legal and Clinical Liability of Comanaging Pediatric Mental Health With Unregulated AI Chatbots
items.author: Hao Yu
items.summary: We conclude that parents and clinicians should proactively discuss chatbot use to promote safety, appropriate expectations, and linkages to evidence-based care.
items.body:
Reply

Ryan K. McBain , Jonathan H. Cantor , Hao Yu

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 16, 2026 Published in: JAMA Pediatrics (2026). DOI: 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.3929

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

In Reply: We thank Lennon for highlighting an issue that requires serious legal and policy attention as adolescents increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for mental health advice. However, we believe the letter rests on a premise that mischaracterizes the conclusions of our article.1 We did not recommend clinicians comanage, police, or actively integrate unregulated chatbots into pediatric mental health care. Rather, we reported that nearly 1 in 5 US adolescents and young adults had used AI chatbots for mental health advice, that most users found them helpful, and that 63.3% disclosed this use to no one. On that basis, we concluded that parents and clinicians should proactively discuss chatbot use to promote safety, appropriate expectations, and linkages to evidence-based care.

items.title: Army Chaplains’ Perceptions About Identifying, Intervening, and Referring Soldiers at Risk of Suicide
items.author: Aaron Kofner
items.summary: In this study, we estimate perceptions of Army chaplains and CAs in domains relevant to gatekeeping, including intervention efficacy, reluctance to intervene, stigma, and past intervention behavior.
items.body:
Rajeev Ramchand , Lynsay Ayer , Lily Geyer , Aaron Kofner

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 16, 2026 Published in: Spirituality in Clinical Practice, Volume 2, No. 1, pages 36-47 (March 2015). DOI: 10.1037/scp0000053

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

In U.S. Army policy, chaplains and chaplain assistants (CAs) are explicitly identified as primary gatekeepers; however, research on their perceptions about their roles identifying, caring for, and referring soldiers in suicidal distress is scant. In this study, we estimate perceptions of Army chaplains and CAs in domains relevant to gatekeeping, including intervention efficacy, reluctance to intervene, stigma, and past intervention behavior. We do so using an online survey that was administered to all chaplains and CAs in the Army’s Active Component and Reserves in 2012. Response rates ranged from 41% of all chaplains in the Active Component to 19% of chaplains and CAs in the Reserves. Almost half of all chaplains and CAs thought they could use more suicide prevention training. Although chaplains reported greater perceived ability to intervene with individuals at risk for suicide relative to civilian samples, they also reported more reluctance to intervene. This reluctance may be explained in part by high reports of stigma regarding mental health treatment. These findings suggest that the Army should implement specific suicide prevention training for chaplains and CAs that focuses on providing acute behavioral health treatment, reducing mental health stigma, and encouraging chaplains to collaborate with other behavioral health resources.

items.title: Evolving Health and Wellbeing of Thalidomide Survivors as They Age
items.author: Agne Ulyte
items.summary: This scoping review updates the 2017 review by exploring evidence published 2017-2025 on the physical, mental, and social wellbeing of ageing thalidomide survivors, identifying emerging health issues, care needs, and evidence gaps.
items.body:
A Scoping Review Update (2017-2025)

Sorana Bucseneanu , Elizabeth Newbronner , Sarah Nettleton , Jennifer Bousfield , Agne Ulyte

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 16, 2026 Published in: Disabilities, Volume 6, Issue 4 (August 2026). DOI: 10.3390/disabilities6040067

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Background

Thalidomide, prescribed to pregnant women in the late 1950s and early 1960s, caused severe congenital impairments known as thalidomide embryopathy, yet the long-term health and wellbeing of survivors as they reach older adulthood remains underexplored.

Objectives

This scoping review updates the 2017 Newbronner and Atkin review by exploring evidence published between 2017 and 2025 on the physical, mental, and social wellbeing of ageing thalidomide survivors, identifying emerging health issues, care needs, and evidence gaps.

Methods

Searches across nine academic databases and grey literature sources identified studies reporting health, wellbeing, or quality of life among middle-aged and older adults with documented prenatal thalidomide exposure.

Results

Thirty papers from the UK, Germany, Japan, Italy, Sweden, Canada, and Australia were included, showing pervasive musculoskeletal deterioration, chronic pain, and increased metabolic disorders. Mental health conditions, including depression, anxiety, and stress, were common and often linked to pain severity and functional limitations, alongside sensory impairments, dental issues, and functional decline, though many survivors demonstrated resilience.

Conclusions

Ageing thalidomide survivors face complex, progressive health challenges that extend beyond congenital impairments, highlighting a need for coordinated, specialist care to support wellbeing in later life.

items.title: Do Stigma and Efficacy Mediate the Association Between Training and Suicide Prevention Behavior Among Army Noncommissioned Officers?
items.author: Lisa Wagner
items.summary: We surveyed Army NCOs to determine if training on suicide prevention and soft skills was associated with gatekeeper behavior and use of soft skills, and whether that association was explained by stigma and perceptions of efficacy.
items.body:
Stephanie Brooks Holliday , Lynsay Ayer , Robin L. Beckman , Lisa H. Jaycox , Denis Agniel , Daniel Elinoff , Rajeev Ramchand , Lisa Wagner

Research Posted on rand.org Sep 16, 2026 Published in: Suicide and Life-Threatening Behavior, Volume 54, Issue 2, pages 195-206 (April 2024). DOI: 10.1111/sltb.13033

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Introduction

Rates of suicide in the Active Component of the military have significantly increased since 2010, with particularly high rates among Army service members. One element of the Army's approach to suicide prevention relies on noncommissioned officers (NCOs) as gatekeepers who have regular contact with soldiers. NCOs receive suicide prevention training, but there is limited evidence that such training leads to behavior change.

Methods

We surveyed 2468 Army NCOs participating in leadership development courses to determine (a) if training on suicide prevention and soft skills (e.g., active listening) was associated with gatekeeper behavior and use of soft skills; and (b) whether that association was explained by two potential barriers, stigma and perceptions of efficacy.

Results

Both the number of suicide prevention training topics and soft skills trained were associated with increased gatekeeper behavior; these relationships were explained in part by lower stigma and higher efficacy for use of soft skills. The use of interactive training methods and receiving coaching after training were not associated with stigma or efficacy, though both methods were associated with more frequent use of soft skills.

Conclusion

Results suggest that the content and format of training is important to preparing NCOs to fulfill a gatekeeper role.

items.title: Preventing the Creation of Mirror Life
items.author: Krista Langeland
items.summary: This brief summarizes RAND research on steps the United States could take to prevent the creation of mirror life—a synthetic life form that could pose irreversible risks—before the window for meaningful action closes.
items.body:
A Strategy for the United States

Nidhi Kalra , Forrest W. Crawford , Matthew L. Nicotra , Scott Behmer , Josh Dettman , Gerald L. Epstein , Edward Geist , David Glickstein , Graham Griffin , Krista Langeland

Research Summary Published Sep 16, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

The creation of mirror life—a hypothetical life form, such as a bacterium, built from biomolecules with the opposite molecular structure of all known life on earth—could cause fatal infections in multicellular life, including humans, animals, and plants, and upend entire ecosystems. In July 2026, RAND published A U.S. Strategy to Prevent the Creation of Mirror Life , which overviews two lines of effort (LOEs) that U.S. policymakers could pursue to prevent mirror life from becoming reality. This brief summarizes these LOEs, the policy levers called for by each LOE, and the principles and analysis on which they are built.

Mirror Life: What It Is and How It Could Pose Catastrophic Risk

Mirror life is a hypothetical form of life built from biomolecules with the opposite molecular structure of all known life on earth. Although mirror life does not yet exist, experts estimate that creation of the first mirror bacterium—a likely first instantiation of mirror life—could be technically feasible within the next few decades and could potentially cost as little as several hundred million dollars.

Mirror life’s reverse molecular structure could enable mirror bacteria to (1) escape immune detection and cause fatal infections, (2) avoid natural predators, and (3) proliferate throughout natural ecosystems. If created and released, whether accidentally or intentionally, mirror bacteria could potentially spread widely, causing irreversible harm.

The Policy Challenge: Preventing an Irreversible Threshold

The policy challenge that mirror life presents is both urgent and unusual. Scientists have produced mirror-image biomolecules that could serve as the building blocks of mirror life. Much of the research that moves science closer to realizing mirror bacteria is not inherently dangerous, has demonstrated benefits or promises benefits, and is likely to continue for reasons unrelated to the creation of mirror life. However, mirror life itself is expected to have few plausible benefits. Despite this, some actors might still wish to pursue mirror life, such as well-intentioned researchers who overlook the risks associated with mirror life or malicious actors who seek to acquire or use mirror life as a doomsday capability.

Traditional governance approaches for emerging technologies—such as post-hoc regulation or adaptive oversight—rely on the opportunity to mitigate risks as they emerge and before they become crises. These approaches might be ill-suited to govern mirror life. This is because once a single viable mirror bacterium exists, the knowledge and methods for making riskier variants could proliferate rapidly, and even seemingly benign strains of such bacteria could be modified to be more dangerous. The first successful creation of mirror life could therefore represent an irreversible threshold: a point after which containment and control become far more difficult and perhaps even impossible.

A Global Challenge Requiring U.S. Leadership

Only a small number of scientifically advanced actors possess the capacity to pursue mirror life. For the foreseeable future, less advanced actors—including isolated or sanctioned regimes, nonstate groups, and individuals—lack the infrastructure, expertise, and access to materials that are required to create mirror life without assistance from the global scientific community. This asymmetry has an important strategic implication: Should the few scientific powers capable of creating mirror life agree on the need to prevent it, their restraint effectively denies the means of creating it to all others.

The United States, as one of the world’s leading scientific powers and a global hub for bioscience and biotechnology, is uniquely positioned to influence the global trajectory of mirror life development and therefore should lead international efforts to prevent its creation. U.S. actions can help establish international restraint, although preventing mirror life ultimately depends on sustained cooperation among the major scientific powers—particularly China—because no country can manage the risk alone.

Four Principles for a U.S. Strategy

RAND researchers guided U.S. policymakers in developing a strategy to address the risks posed by mirror life before scientific progress or geopolitical incentives close the window for meaningful action. Rather than predicting whether mirror life will pose catastrophic risk with certainty, the authors treat the expert assessment that mirror life could pose unacceptable risks as sufficient motivation for strategic planning now.

RAND researchers identified the following four principles, which guide the development of a strategy:

Prevention over mitigation: Because the first mirror bacterium could trigger irreversible consequences and enable the rapid proliferation of mirror life capabilities, governance, norms, and constraints must be established before mirror life exists—rather than governments and other actors relying on mitigation after the fact.

Universal restraint over partial restraint: Even a single actor creating mirror life could pose a global risk. Prevention depends on broadly shared restraint supported by coordinated governance, transparency, and scientific norms.

Transparency over secrecy: A shared understanding of mirror life’s risks and confidence that others are exercising restraint are essential for preventing competitive dynamics and sustaining collective prevention efforts.

Cooperation over coercion: Because no country can eliminate the risk alone, prevention requires trusted international cooperation that preserves legitimacy and encourages broad participation rather than coercive measures.

Two Lines of Effort: Reducing Incentives and Advancing Detection and Deterrence

RAND researchers identified policy levers that policymakers could consider, specifically those that (1) reduce incentives to develop mirror life and (2) detect and deter early-stage development of mirror life. Other levers—such as those that disrupt or punish advanced development or build countermeasures and resilience—are inconsistent with the four strategic principles and therefore do not factor into a U.S. preventive strategy.

The U.S. strategy organizes levers into the following LOEs (Figure 1):

LOE 1—Engage scientific superpowers, especially China, to build the foundation for collective restraint. This LOE prioritizes transparent scientific collaboration, shared risk assessments, and early norm-setting to discourage major powers from viewing mirror life as a strategic advantage and to prevent mirror life research from becoming an arena for geopolitical competition. LOE 1 shapes the incentives for major scientific powers and academic institutions and has a cascading impact on other nation-states and commercial firms. Although LOE 1’s direct influence on other actors is more limited, broadly stigmatizing mirror life could still create reputational and operational barriers for malign actors.

LOE 2—Establish collective restraint across domestic, allied, and competing scientific communities. This LOE combines measures that reduce the incentives and increase the costs of creating mirror life. Together, these actions shift motivations and capabilities away from mirror life development for states, commercial firms, research institutions, and multilateral bodies.

In pursuing these LOEs, the United States should:

Commit clearly to not developing mirror life, even if other actors are suspected of pursuing it. This commitment reflects the fact that the possession of mirror life would not provide protection, deterrence, or resilience against mirror life developed by others and would instead exacerbate global risk.

Take great caution with actions or statements that could foster mistrust or spur strategic competition in the field of mirror life or its enabling technologies, particularly actions or statements that are related to disrupting mirror life development or investing in countermeasures and resilience.

Advance actions with longer lead times as soon as possible. Legislation, international engagement, technology development for detection and verification, and treaty-creation groundwork require years to mature. These efforts should begin now and evolve as new information emerges.

Exclude coercive measures from the strategy at this time. Actions that rely on pressure, disruption, or punishment would erode trust and cooperation among major scientific powers on which prevention depends. Such measures should be out of scope at this time. If such measures ever become appropriate, they should be pursued cooperatively and transparently, not unilaterally.

Treat countermeasures and resilience as later-resort measures. These measures are unlikely to be effective against the proliferation of mirror life and the ensuing risks. Premature or unilateral investment in defensive preparations could inadvertently weaken deterrence, advance the science of mirror life, and trigger counterproductive dynamics.

By strengthening trust, transparency, and cooperative incentives, the United States can help ensure that those with the means to develop mirror life choose not to—and, in doing so, make mirror life’s pursuit infeasible for everyone else.

items.title: The Insurability of Artificial Intelligence
items.author: Celine Robinson
items.summary: A mismatch exists between rapid enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and the market for insuring it. This report examines AI incidents, lawsuits, laws, and insurance filings to assess coverage responses and accumulation risks.
items.body:
A mismatch exists between rapid enterprise adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and the fragmented market for insuring AI-related losses. This report examines AI incidents, U.S. lawsuits, enacted state laws, and insurance filings to assess how insurers are responding through exclusions, endorsements, affirmative coverage, or silence.

The Insurability of Artificial Intelligence

Sasha Romanosky , Celine Robinson

Research Published Sep 16, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Businesses increasingly embed artificial intelligence (AI) in operations, products, and services, creating both new opportunities and new forms of risk. Firms are deploying AI in customer service, employment screening, coding, fraud detection, and autonomous systems. At the same time, AI-related harms are already emerging, including incorrect or misleading outputs, deepfakes, privacy violations, intellectual property disputes, fraud, product defects, and discriminatory decisions. These harms create demand for insurance but do not fit neatly within existing insurance lines.

In this report, the authors examine AI incidents, U.S. lawsuits, enacted state laws, and admitted-market insurance filings to assess how insurers are responding through exclusions, endorsements, affirmative coverage, or silence. Key findings include the dominance of misinformation incidents, concentration of litigation around intellectual property, and five mechanisms through which AI could generate accumulation losses across insurance lines.

Key Takeaways

Of public generative AI incidents, 84 percent relate to misinformation (false, deceptive, or manipulative content) and deepfakes (AI-generated or altered media impersonating a real person or event).

Of U.S. litigation for generative AI harms, 60 percent relate to the alleged violations of intellectual property or improper training by AI developers rather than to the use, misuse, or outputs of these models.

Most U.S. states have adopted laws focusing on restricting harmful synthetic content, such as nonconsensual intimate images and child sexual abuse material.

Unlike cyber, AI risks are not contained to a single insurance line but span many lines: technology errors and omissions and professional liability, cyber, directors and officers, commercial property, and more.

Insurance carriers are responding to AI risks unevenly, with some offering affirmative coverage for certain risks (e.g., model errors), and others filing broad exclusions for any AI-related loss.

Most carriers are remaining silent, neither affirming nor excluding AI-related risks in their policies, leaving coverage for such losses untested and open to dispute.

Recommendations

State insurance regulators and the National Association of Insurance Commissioners, supported by carriers and brokers, should develop an AI Coverage Notice enabling carriers to clarify how, and under which lines, AI-related losses are affirmatively covered, excluded, or left silent.

Incident reporting for attritional and accumulation loss should be standardized. Policy researchers and brokers, together with carriers and reinsurers, should develop a common, adaptable taxonomy for AI incidents, claims, and controls to properly track and report on AI risks. Actual incident data should remain private, however.

Insurers and reinsurers should analyze AI aggregation scenarios, focusing on shared model dependency, common infrastructure failure, and regulatory shock to manage correlated AI risk.

items.title: Positioning Qatar in the Global Research, Development, and Innovation Landscape
items.author: Sara Zikri
items.summary: Qatar aims to strengthen its research, development, and innovation (RDI) ecosystem. This report benchmarks Qatar against other small advanced economies and identifies policy options to close gaps in STEM talent, research, and innovation capacity.
items.body:
Qatar aims to strengthen its research, development, and innovation (RDI) ecosystem. This report benchmarks Qatar against other small advanced economies, examines international policy practices, and evaluates its national strategies. It identifies weak STEM interest, fragmented researcher support, retention challenges linked to short visas, and limited industry–academia collaboration, and sets out policy options to address these gaps.

Positioning Qatar in the Global Research, Development, and Innovation Landscape

Comparative Insights from Small Advanced Economies

Mehdi Shiva , James Besse , Stella Harrison , Miguel Subosa , Ishita Puri , Paul Khullar , Abdellahi Hussein , Sara Zikri

Research Published Sep 16, 2026

Share on LinkedIn

Share on X

Share on Facebook

Qatar has articulated a bold vision to strengthen its research, development, and innovation (RDI) ecosystem, as set out in the Third National Development Strategy and the Qatar Research Development and Innovation Council's 2030 Strategy. These strategies set ambitious targets for expanding the RDI talent pool, raising government investment in research and innovation, and improving outputs such as high-impact publications, patents and start-ups.

This report assesses the current state of Qatar's RDI ecosystem by benchmarking performance indicators against other small, advanced economies, examining international policy practices, and evaluating the effects of Qatar's national strategies on research and innovation outcomes. It highlights areas of relative strength and identifies policy options to address persistent gaps.

The most significant challenge identified is the relatively low level of interest and attainment in STEM disciplines among Qatari students, which weakens the domestic talent pipeline. Although national strategies recognise the importance of STEM education, a comprehensive and coordinated action plan is lacking. Support for early-career researchers is also fragmented, and retention of skilled international talent is constrained by short visa durations and limited employment flexibility. Collaboration between research institutions and the private sector remains limited, restricting the translation of knowledge into innovation.

The study finds that the Qatar National Vision 2030 has positively influenced research and innovation outputs, even amid regional and global disruptions, and the more recent QRDI 2030 Strategy shows early signs of effectiveness, though it is too soon to assess its full impact. Future evaluations should incorporate broader indicators and longitudinal data.

Key Takeaways

Industry–academia collaboration is limited

Linkages between research institutions and the private sector remain weak, constraining the translation of knowledge into innovation. While the business set-up process is relatively streamlined, set-up costs have been high relative to comparator economies, standing at 6.3% of GNI per capita in 2019, though recent developments suggest significant reductions. Against a backdrop of declining total factor productivity, revitalising the private sector through entrepreneurship and innovation is increasingly important. Existing infrastructure such as QSTP and Education City offers a foundation on which closer co-location and coordination between academia and industry can be built.

Researcher development and retention need targeted attention

Support for early-career researchers is fragmented and administered largely by individual universities, producing variable training quality. Recent visa reforms, including the Mustaqel visa and the abandonment of the Kafala system, have improved conditions for migrant researchers, but short visa durations and limited employment flexibility continue to push international talent away, often before researchers can secure subsequent employment.

STEM interest and attainment remain weak

The relatively low level of interest and attainment in STEM disciplines among Qatari students weakens the domestic talent pipeline and limits capacity to meet future workforce demands. Despite improvements in attainment over the past decade, Qatar continues to underperform in science and mathematics relative to other small, advanced economies. National strategies acknowledge STEM's importance, but no concrete, coordinated action plan is in place.

Recommendations

A more coordinated approach to STEM education

Qatar may wish to consider a coordinated STEM action plan spanning early to adult education, with clearer roles and stronger teacher development. Finland and New Zealand's teacher-led communities of practice offer useful reference points.

Supporting researcher development and retention

There may be value in exploring a nationally administered fellowship scheme for early-career researchers, drawing on Singapore's approach, alongside greater visa flexibility informed by models such as Ireland's.

Deepening industry–academia collaboration

Building on QSTP and Education City, Qatar could consider cluster-based approaches, with QRDI well placed to help coordinate and evaluate support.
